speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you look at the Projected Order of Business, it says:
Note: Length of speeches, pursuant to Standing Order 35(1):
-unlimited time-Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition -20-minute maximum (all other speakers)
-all speeches are subject to 10-minute question and comment period.
If this is the case, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that the motion which is about to be moved by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) is not limited to a debate not extending more than two hours. Otherwise, we would certainly not find the Order Paper constructed in the way it is. As you have pointed out to us previously, Sir, Standing Order 82 calls for only 10-minute speeches. However, it is clear from the very clear wording of the Notice Paper today that if the speeches are pursuant to Standing Order 35(1), I respectfully submit that there is not then a two hour time limit on debate of this motion. I thought it was important to bring this to your attention at the very outset of the debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member. The Hon. Member is indeed correct that if it were a motion under 35(1) there would indeed be unlimited debate. I have a note to myself to indicate this before anybody said anything else. I appreciate the point. Therefore, before putting the question on the motion to the House, may I, for the benefit of Hon. Members, indicate that the time allowed for speeches on the motion as listed on today's Projected Order of Business is incorrect. In fact, the provisions of Standing Order 82 apply and all speeches will be limited to 10 minutes. As a consequence, two hours after
commencement of proceedings on the motion, the question shall be put to the House. The motion is properly under Standing Order 82.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sinclair Stevens (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the following proposed motion:
That, further to the notice given on Thursday, May 2, 1985 by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, and pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 82, in relation to Bill C-15, An Act respecting investment in Canada, one sitting day shall be allotted to the consideration of each of the report stage and the third reading stage of the said bill; and
That fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business on those days, any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted, if necessary, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary to dispose of the stage of the bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate I would like to begin by saying that, pursuant to Standing Order 82, there is now time allocation which will have the effect of requiring that there be only one sitting day at report stage of Bill C-15, and one sitting day at third reading stage of the same Bill. There may be those who ask why we felt it necessary to bring in time allocation. I can only say to such people that if they had had an opportunity to sit in the House and watch the progress of Bill C-15 at second reading and at committee stage and if they had seen the stalling and filibustering tactics which the Official Opposition and the NDP Members used, they would be endorsing this time allocation motion.
I would like to refer specifically to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) made recently in this Chamber. He said, "We are prepared to spend as many hours, days or weeks in the House debating these matters as required". The unfortunate thing, Mr. Speaker, is that the Hon. Member was not kidding. If the Opposition had its way we would still be debating Bill C-15 this time next year, or even the year after that. We would be going over the same ground, hearing the same arguments, and having amendments put which had already been duly considered and in many cases voted down in the committee which made a very in-depth study of this Bill.
If Hon. Members read some of the arguments used, I think they would find them to be hackneyed, trite and, what is most unforgivable, ignoring the hard fact that there are 1.5 million Canadians out of work who would like to see investment, preferably from Canadian sources, but certainly from all sources, considered with a view to creating the prosperity and jobs which the country needs. It is beyond reason to claim that insufficient time has been allowed for debate on this legisla-

May 21, 1985
Time Allocation
tion. We have already devoted many hours to it, both in the House and in committee.
Let me emphasize again how much time has been spent. In that respect, I would like to compare the number of Members we have heard speaking on Bill C-15 with the number who spoke on the Foreign Investment Review Bill back in 1973. At second reading of Bill C-15, there were 72 speakers, compared to only 26 speakers at the second reading of the Foreign Investment Review Bill. A total of 128 speakers have spoken so far at the report stage of Bill C-15, compared to only 68 at the report stage of the Foreign Investment Review Bill.
What a contrast! When one thinks of it, the Foreign Investment Review Act changed Canada's attitude toward nonCanadian investment in a very fundamental way. It was a true policy change. If the House saw fit to pass that type of legislation, surely it is rather remarkable, ten years after the fact, when we bring in legislation that we think is improving the approach, still putting in meaningful review where necessary while making it clear that we welcome Canadian and non-Canadian investment, that those in the Opposition now feel their right is to block such legislation and delay it much more than ever was the case with respect to the original Foreign Investment Review Act.
In the House last week, my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay), and I spelled out the number of hours spent in debate on Bill C-15. Let me repeat them once again for the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry and the other hard of hearing socialists on the opposition benches. It has now become crystal clear that every reasonable point that could have been raised in regard to Bill C-15 has indeed been raised. At second reading, the Bill received 15 hours of debate in the House, a total of 40 hours in committee and a total of almost 24 hours at report stage up to and including May 2. How can the Opposition claim that we have not provided enough time for the consideration of their important and constructive amendments? This argument, like so many of their arguments, is simply ludicrous.
It has now become crystal clear that every reasonable and constructive point to be raised with regard to Bill C-15 has already been raised. Several opposition motions which were rejected in the committee were still put forward here in the House. Obviously it was a stalling tactic. Furthermore, several of the opposition motions put forward in the House have been ruled out of order.
Opposition Members may be smug in the knowledge that their attempts to obstruct passage of this vital piece of legislation has worked so far. Are they equally smug in the knowledge that at the same time they are obstructing the economic progress of the Canadians who elected us all? I can tell you of one group who do not appreciate this smugness. They are the workers who are looking for jobs in this country. They feel that such stalling on a meaningful approach to future investment in Canada is not what the Parliament of Canada should be a party to. In short, they believe that it is time to allow the will
of the majority of the electors, as evidenced in the last election, to be recorded in the House of Commons and presumably in the other place.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext:
In short, it is our view that we must start facing the facts. We must remove needless obstacles to investment in this country in order to bring to Canada the capital, the technology development, the industrial growth and, above all, those new jobs to which I have been referring this morning.
To remove needless barriers to investment here is precisely the way we have drafted Bill C-15. By proposing this legislation, the Government of Canada is saying to Canadians, "Let us try out new ideas and technology. Let us work together, federal and provincial Governments, public and private sectors, to put Canada on the road to economic recovery. Let us demonstrate the Canadian edge in energy, technology, markets, growth, people, and ideas". The time has come to put an end to the Opposition's endless talking about this Bill. The time has come for action. The time has come to pass Bill C-15.
Canada needs the benefit that this legislation can provide. It is our responsibility to bring the benefits within our reach by passing this Bill as expeditiously as possible.
May I remind all members of the Opposition that the Progressive Conservative Party made a commitment to Canada, to the Canadian electors during the election, to replace the Foreign Investment Review Act with a simpler, less restrictive investment policy. We were elected to carry out the will of Canadians. We intend to see it carried out with precision and purpose. We will not be held back by an Opposition bent on disruption for the sake of disruption. That is why I have introduced this motion to limit debate at this point. We will not see this Bill and with it Canada's economic recovery put on hold.
In short, any Member who decides to resist, to vote against this legislation, is contributing to the lack of investment in Canada and, unfortunately, to the ultimate lack of jobs for Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext: Nonsense. Such total nonsense.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister in introducing this closure motion said that the time has come. I think that was his resounding refrain. That is the one statement with which I can agree. The time has now come when the Canadian people will see this new Conservative Government exposed for what it really is, namely, made up of a group of hypocrites.

They are a group of people who have in the past stood in the House of Commons with the most self-righteous indignation, proclaiming the right of Parliament to open and free debate about the important issues of the time. These
May 21, 1985

are the people who held up parliamentary debate for two solid weeks on the Constitution with bell ringing tactics. On the debate on the Western Grain Transportation Act they maintained close to nine months of debate. We had a report stage that lasted 15 weeks, and they introduced over 100 amendments. At that time what they did was an exercise in democratic right. Now when we get to the foreign investment question which deals with billions of dollars of economic development, this Government is no longer prepared to tolerate Parliament exercising its rightful role.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext: What about jobs?

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext:
The most supercilious proposition put forward since this Government came to power is contained in the statements made by the Minister that the reason for this thrust is only that the Conservatives want to help the working people, or the people who want to work, the 1.5 million who are unemployed. Everyone in this House wants to help them. The problem-and this is what the Minister does not understand- is that he has not made the case. His problem is that, because of the weakness of his own arguments and the lack of presentation by members of his own caucus who refuse to debate, they have not made the case.
The poll done last night was prime proof. The majority of Canadians do not want further foreign ownership. You have failed, Sir, to show and to demonstrate how this Bill in any way, shape or form will be able to assist: Canadians to get jobs. The problem is that we have a basic fallacy on our hands. Parliament is being asked to pass a Bill based upon pure fiction. Time after time witnesses appeared before the committee and gave arguments that the Bill would make no difference and there would not be a great onrush of new capital as a result of it. When representatives of the New York money markets were interviewed and asked whether it would make a big difference, they said: "No, of course not".
[DOT] (M20)
Last year we had $4 billion worth of foreign investment come into the country. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) is a man who lives totally in mythology; he has no reality about him. One of his great mythologies is that somehow this is night and day; that there was no foreign investment before and there will be foreign investment now. He does not read the reports of his own agencies, which indicated that last year there was close to $4 billion worth of foreign investment coming into Canada. The difference is that that foreign investment came in to create jobs in Canada. Repeatedly in the course of this debate we have indicated that with total free licence and lack of any kind of bargaining power, the foreign investment which the Minister is inviting into the country will take away the jobs and opportunities of Canadian workers. He should ask the workers in Canadian Porcelain whether they think foreign investment is a good deal. He should ask one of his own Members who jumped to his feet in high dudgeon last week to ask: "What about Irwin-Dor-sey?" A foreign owner closed down that plant in his riding and
Time Allocation
took away 35 jobs from that area. Time after time we have seen the same example.
Without conditions being negotiated, without some agreement on the part of foreign investors that when they come to Canada they will provide a clear commitment to secure jobs, to provide an opportunity for the Canadian-based subsidiary to conduct research and development and recognize the right of that Canadian subsidiary to get into the world export market, without those kinds of guarantees, the Canadian economy is the poorer for foreign investment. The one hard, clear, undeniable piece of evidence which was repeatedly raised was that unless we are able to secure those guarantees, Canadian subsidiaries will perform far less well economically for Canadians than Canadian-owned companies. They import much more, which substantially affects our ability to sell and our balance of payments. Their mandate in export markets is far less, and they conduct far less research and development. That is the evidence which this Opposition has been trying to impress upon the Minister. The problem is that the Minister is so close-minded, so obdurate, so insensitive and so absolutely disdainful of the role of Parliament that he does not bother to listen or to respond.
The Minister does not care about what other people have to say. We have seen this time and time again. Even when there are partisan differences, the primary role of the committee structure and report stage is to try to make the Bill better than that which the Government initially presented. Parliament is not here as a rubber-stamp. It is not here for government Members to flap their wings in wild applause. It is here to do an honest and effective job in trying to make a piece of legislation more effective and more useful. The Minister does not understand that process.
There is no question that the other side was given a mandate in the last election to bring about a change in the Foreign Investment Review Agency. That change should have been subject to the salutary, beneficial effect of a proper parliamentary process, but we have a Minister who does not believe in it. Therefore he refused to accept any amendments, refused to conduct any negotiations and refused to deal with the kinds of representations we heard. He is a Minister who does not care about Parliament, and that is part of the case we are making. Of course, we must bring forward a number of amendments because those brought forward at committee stage were totally rejected and there were only 14 sessions of the committee.

He should read his parliamentary history before he flaps his lips. The fact of the matter is that Parliament is here to provide judgment and assessment in order to make the process more constructive.

While trying to make his definitive case, the Minister said that there were fewer speakers when we debated the Foreign Investment Review Agency. Why is that? It is because there was more consensus in the House on that legislation than there is on this legislation. The Minister does not understand Parliament. Other Parties were supportive of that legislation and were prepared to give it a try.
This Minister has not been listening very well. He has not even listened to some of the key questions. For example, we asked a question regarding the arbitrary discretionary power of one Minister to make billions of dollars worth of investments. We asked if he should not be required to consult from time to time with his colleagues in caucus. We saw what the Minister did regarding Domtar. We know how he had to have his wrist slapped by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and members of the Quebec caucus so that he would change his mind. We will see a repetition of that case time and time again.
We have a wilful, headstrong Minister who does not care about the opinions or judgments of those in other regions. We know of the Minister's history in western Canada. He was the great creator of the Bank of Western Canada. We know how much he cares about regional interest in that area of the country. We know how much he cares about Domtar in Quebec. We are simply saying that for the sake of God, Parliament should put some restraint on the wilful arbitrariness of one Minister. However, the Minister has not bothered to listen to us. That is okay with us because we know the kind of hot water in which he and the Government will be time and time again.
This debate is about the fact that the Minister and the Government do not care about Parliament. The Government is not prepared to use the parliamentary process the way it was designed to be used. That will tell the Canadian people far more than anything else about just what kind of Government they elected. They elected a Government that is presidential rather than parliamentary in style, and that will be its downfall.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a sad and shameful day when the Minister can stand before the House to claim with self-righteousness that he is somehow meeting the needs of the Canadian people by closing off debate on this Bill. I want to-

speechtext: It's your speech.

speechtext:
If my speech has the capacity to strike terror into the heart of the Minister, I will be pleased indeed.
If we could, let us talk about honesty. Let us talk about what has actually occurred with respect to this debate. I would
like to review those facts for the House because I think there must be Members of the House who are not aware of them since they applaud so vociferously what this Minister is doing.
First, let us talk about the committee hearings which were held with respect to this Bill. The Minister likes to suggest that somehow those committee hearings gave everyone across the country a chance to comment, to have input and to consult, to use the favourite phrase of the Government. The reality is that at least 28 witnesses who wanted to testify before that committee were prevented from doing so. Most of those witnesses were the kind of disinterested witnesses who would have been able to offer a great deal in terms of non-partisan advice with respect to this Bill. The Director of the Research Centre at Queens University and-dare I say it-the son of the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton), people such as they who have a certain perspective based on detailed study and a lack of access to grants, did not approach the subject with the extreme prejudice of the Minister. They were cut off and not permitted to testify.
We could move from the witness stage to the stage at which amendments were reviewed. Again, the Minister tells us that the committee was able to study with care and diligence all the suggestions which were made by opposition Members. That was not so. There were only three days of debate. At least half of the amendments which were put before the committee were not debated. Then the Bill, at report stage, came to the House. Again the Government is suggesting that a filibuster is taking place.
If we look at the debates which have taken place on each of the sets of amendments which have been brought forward, we Find that there has been a reasonable number of speakers. There are 30 people in the NDP caucus, but in no case have we offered 30 speakers. In most cases we have not come close.
These are key items. The Minister spoke about his mandate to see the Bill through the House. Indeed, he has that mandate. In principle, the people of the country supported the notion of Investment Canada, but they did not vote last September to have no public input to the hearings which are held on Investment Canada. The people of Canada did not vote to have ineffective criteria on which to judge companies. For instance, there is no criterion to look at the financial viability of the parent companies of the firms which are taking over Canadian companies. The people of Canada did not vote for a definition of assets which is totally confusing. It will provide a bonanza for lawyers, but it will not give Canadians the protection which they deserve when takeovers occur.
In report stage on the Bill, we are dealing with key technical points. Surely to God each of those points is worthy of some debate. Yet the House will be given only one day to look at the important amendments which remain.
The Minister claims that what he is doing is designed to protect workers in Canada and to find jobs for the future. There are many points of view concerning the question of foreign investment. On the basis of experience I would hold

May 21, 1985

that the Minister's view is faulty and that the analysis which lies behind it is mistaken. But that is something on which we can differ. That is not what is at debate at report stage. We are not debating that broad principle at report stage. We are debating a whole set of crucial amendments, such as amendments concerning changes which would ensure that branches of U.S. companies, if they change hands, are subject to review. If, for instance, the Iron Ore Company of Canada changed hands, which threatened jobs for Canadian workers, there is no capacity in the present Bill to review the takeover, because of faults in the organization of the Bill. Branches are not included, but subsidiaries are. That is one example of the kinds of technical but important points which deserve careful scrutiny before the House votes on the important amendments brought forward.
There are several cases which have come before us since September, such as those of Black & Decker, Mitel and Canadian Porcelain. In each of those cases, the importance to Canadian workers in being able to turn to the Foreign Investment Review Agency for protection or to safeguard their positions, has been an important ingredient in the economic future of Canada. This Bill will eliminate that protection for many workers. In that sense, it is absolute and total nonsense to say that this Bill somehow meets the needs of the 1.5 million people who are unemployed. In fact, those people are threatened by the rationalizations that may take place as takeovers occur and foreign investments leave Canada as branch plants shut down and subsidiaries restructure. The Minister should remember this day in the future when he faces case after case of shut-downs of Canadian subsidiaries and of the rationalization associated with North American free trade. Day after day he will face the sense of loss which his Bill leaves among the workers and the communities.
On election night we had a sense of hope. Instead of hope, today we have a sense of shame as the Government uses its large power to stifle debate. We see a sense of dishonesty as arguments are brought forward which are not appropriate to report stage of the Bill. We feel a sense of sadness. The Government controls all power in the House of Commons. It can do what it wants to do. But on behalf of my Party I want to register the sadness and the sense of regret which we feel as this Government adopts the arrogance, the sense of overweening pride, and the sense of dominance and concern with its own policies and beliefs at the exclusion of ideas and input from opposition Parties which so marked the Government voted out of office last September.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a few comments on the motion to limit debate on this Bill and to respond to a few of the assertions which have been made by the two previous speakers. I found it interesting to listen to the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) and the obvious sincerity, albeit very often misguided, with which he speaks. The remarks of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry certainly speak for themselves and will later be addressed.
Time Allocation
There are several obvious reasons for this motion to limit debate on Bill C-15. The time which has been spent on this Bill has been addressed by previous speakers. As the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) previously stated, the time spent on debate in the House and in committee is now approaching 80 hours. I believe that Canadians who are watching the proceedings of the House of Commons can appreciate what 80 hours of discussion should be able to generate and accomplish. There has been extensive participation in debate by all Members in the House and in committee. It was interesting that one of the member of the Opposition commented on, in his words, the "stifling" of people in committee. There were 23 representations made in committee for a total of 26 hours of discussion. There were 30 additional briefs and 19 amendments accepted by the committee. These amendments, briefs, submissions, and representations dealt exhaustively and extensively with the Bill.
There has also been concern expressed, as mentioned by the Hon. Minister, about the obstruction of popular will. On September 4 the Government received a massive mandate from Canadians who had many desires and aspirations for their Government. The people of Canada look toward the Government for some new and innovative approaches to the economy. The Minister's Bill has drawn a very sensible and equitable balance between the Government and those Canadians and non-Canadians who wish to invest in our country. The needless number of amendments proposed by the Opposition would have reinstated FIRA and gone much further to undermine the popular will of Canadians.
What did Canadians want on September 4 in the area of investment by non-Canadians? They clearly showed that they did not want the intervention exercised by the past Government. The over 90 amendments moved by the Opposition went even further than asking for the reinstatement of FIRA. The Opposition debate to this point has been repetitive, to say the least. As Canadians watch the parliamentary proceedings, they find it sad that the House of Commons has become a "talk shop".
The NDP espouses a philosophy and point of view that is, to say the least, unrealistic. I hearken back to my province of Saskatchewan. When one grows up in the only province which has had over 40 years of New Democratic and CCF Governments, one learns very quickly the extent to which that Party wants the state involved in the lives of all people.
It is unfortunate that the opposition Parties have used the number of hours that they have. Liberals have spoken 82 times in the House on Bill C-15. New Democrats have been on their feet 72 times. These interventions made simply reiterate tired and meaningless amendments which waste the time of Canadian people who are watching the proceedings of the House. Debate in the House is often compared to a freeway. There are all sorts of Bills affecting farmers, native people, and other Canadians in the merge lane trying to get into the House of Commons. Yet debate in the House is taken up by an Opposi-

May 21, 1985
Time Allocation
tion which makes many interventions and amendments which border on the frivolous. For that reason, the House of Commons is not being used in the responsible fashion in which it should.

Those who wish to invest in Canada look at the positive aspects of the Investment Canada Bill and wonder why it cannot clear the House of Commons. They wonder why the Opposition is causing such a delay. We are not doing a service to the people who wish to invest in Canada.
For that reason I speak in support of this motion to limit time for debate. Owing to its sense of democracy, the Government has allowed the fullest airing of opinions on this Bill. The committee has dealt with this matter extensively and it is now time to move on to other pressing matters that are before the House of Commons.
I would like to address some comments through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), who speaks about hypocrisy. It makes the heart flip and the stomach turn to hear that Member talk about hypocrisy.

The pot calling the kettle black had nothing on the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. Unction oozes from every pore of his little body. He speaks with a sanctimonious air about what his political Party stands for and what his Government did. After the years of pitiful, sad performance by his Government, with him as a Minister, this is neither the time nor the place for members of the Liberal Party to discuss hypocrisy.
It was interesting to hear Liberal Members saying that we should leave FIRA as it is because it did not prevent anything; that the majority of proposals were simply rubber-stamped. They wanted FIRA because they could use it as a political football. The Liberal Party wanted to use people's hopes, concerns and views about investment as a political football to play upon feelings of economic nationalism from time to time. When it got a little too repressive it would simply back off on FIRA and economic nationalism. The blatant political overtones of FIRA were seen for what they were on September 4.
I call upon Members of the House to support the proposal to bring Bill C-15 to a vote and to move on to the other important issues which await the people of Canada. For that reason I support this motion of time allocation to enable the House to move on to other serious matters which await us.

But that is not my point. My point is that the Conservatives did not have an agenda, they did not have anything on the books. All they had was Investment Canada. And when we said, let's work together and improve this legislation, they said no. They said they were going to cut off debate, have only two hours of ten-minute speeches following which we are going to vote, and of course, "We have the majority", as they put it so well. "We are 211. We are the bullies on the street, we are going to tell Canadians how we run this country." Watch out on Thursday. Every night for the last two weeks we have heard that it is going to be a tough Budget. Be careful, Canadians, you are really going to get it. But on Thursday they will say, "We are a bunch of nice guys". Such beautiful marketing, but what a bunch of nonsense!
Let us look at the amendments and what the Minister called the obstructionist Liberals. We proposed that the Minister
May 21, 1985

should give policy direction to the agency. Did he accept that? No. It is going to be another part of his office. No direction there. They will do whatever he decides. And if some foreign company comes over and wants to buy anything in Canada, it is welcome to it. The Minister is the only one who will decide. He will not even have to consult his Cabinet colleagues. Great. Well, I say that is not the way things should be. Motion No. 6 suggests that finding Canadian buyers should be a duty of the Minister. Sure, we want foreign investment, but we should ensure that Canadians buy into their own economy. Last week I heard a Member saying that in Canadians' minds FIRA is not important any more. But before they start to snap their suspenders, as we say in French-peter les bretelles-I would remind them that the reason Canadians-

-the reason why Canadians are not concerned about FIRA is because the agency has been a good thing for Canada. For instance, in 1970, as Canadians are aware, the manufacturing sector was 61 per cent foreign-owned. By 1980, this percentage had dropped to 53 per cent. We had recovered 8 per cent of our economy. The same thing was true-

That is not true. We did not close the shop but we made Canadians take an interest in the shop.
In 1970, 76 per cent of oil and natural gas interests were in foreign hands. By 1980, this was 51 per cent. Why? Because we gave Canadians the challenge of becoming the masters of their economy and increasing their participation in the economy by buying back our resources and our companies.

In mining and smelting foreign ownership decreased from 80 per cent to 48 per cent in the period from 1970 to 1980. I thought that was pretty good. So FIRA was useful. Of course Canadians said in the latest poll that they are not too preoccupied with FIRA being modified. I can understand that because we reached a certain level of Canadianization with FIRA; you have to admit that. We reversed a trend which was quite disquieting to many of us, where foreign ownership was becoming a threat to our economy. As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) said, they are companies that are welcome, but we know from observing their practices that they do not do the same amount of research and development as do Canadian companies in Canada.
We would like to develop our high-tech industry, we would like to think that the Mitels and the Gandalfs and the Nabus and all these small companies will some day be able to compete in the international sphere, but with Canadian ownership being guaranteed. I do not think there is anything wrong with that. What is there in this Bill to encourage Canadians to invest in their own economy? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. What is there in this Bill that will interest foreigners to come in and invest in Canadian manufacturing industries and the
Time Allocation
Canadian economy? Nothing. Except that the Government, through a campaign of-

"Denigration", I do not know the right expression in English, so I use this one, a campaign to denigrate FIRA. They spread the view around that the agency was a threat to this country's economy, that it was responsible for the economic crisis we experienced following the recession of 1980, 1981 and 1982. But that is just not true! It was the international economic situation. In order to finance a very substantial deficit, the Americans increased interest rates in the U.S. to such high levels that foreign capital flooded into the United States. I remember last year when, in three months, $40 billion were invested in the United States. Why? Because they were paying 13 and 14 per cent, that is why. So this money was not going to Canada, and Canadians with money to invest were going to put it where? Where they were likely to get the best return on their investment, and this was happening on an international scale.
You do not have to be an economic genius to understand that all this was not FIRA's fault, that it did not cause the economic recession. Of course the agency was affected in recent years, but last year, 97 per cent of FIRA applications were approved in Canada. This means $4.1 billion worth of foreign capital was invested in this country, created jobs, and breathed new life into an economy that needed a boost, so that today, Canadians are capable of defending themselves and fighting their own battles. It seems that the responsible Minister who is going to be the czar or the big boss of the new agency is going to be the only one to decide what goes. It seems he will not have to consult with his Cabinet colleagues and will be able to do what he wants, when he wants. I say this is very disturbing, because there are companies like Mitel which received as much as $30 million in grants from the Federal Government for the purpose of expansion, and I am thinking of Renfrew and Buctouche, and there is going to be a lot more said about this matter. They got grants! I say that a Canadian company that gets federal grants should be screened by the Foreign Investment Review Agency, but now, the Minister will not have to bother about that. He will not do that anymore. He will choose who he wants. Come on in, we are for sale, and we are a terrific bargain!
Mr. Speaker, so much for my comments. I will get back to the amendments later on.

The public's reaction is positive. That is what counts. It is a matter of

attitude and confidence. We have restored that confidence and we must go on. I was interested in the comments made by the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley). I yearn for the days when his predecessor said intelligent things here. In fact, I hear from those who normally vote Tory in Saskatchewan that they can hardly wait for the next election to return the former Member to his place in the House.
I do not want to make any apologies for what we are doing. The Government does not have an agenda of programs to bring forward. If it had programs, we would not have had six consecutive opposition days in the House. I tell the government Members not to give us that malarkey. Don't give us that malarkey about the Government wanting to get on with the business of Canada by bringing forward its programs to solve the very serious problems confronting the people of Canada.
The Government does not have programs to bring forward, and this is why we were forced to put up speaker after speaker to give our views on how the country ought to be run. The Conservative party was either afraid or unwilling to put up speakers to demonstrate its ideas. That has been the problem with this Parliament. I do not heap that abuse on new Members because I do not expect them to have particularly good ideas. Most of them did not expect to be elected in the first place.
With respect to the Government's present action, I believe that it is fundamental that we take every step necessary to preserve the integrity of this nation economically and socially. It is on our shoulders in this Parliament to do whatever we can to ensure that there will in fact be the kind of economic opportunities and social integrity that Canada has fought and struggled so hard to maintain for many years. What this Government is doing through this legislation is undermining that very purpose. I think that is what makes it so offensive to us on this side of the House.
It is true that FIRA was not all that it could have been. It is true that FIRA did not measure up in many ways to what
Time Allocation
some of us had anticipated it might do. It is also true that although FIRA was in place, there were a large number of takeovers about which I had some serious reservations and about which many of my colleagues had serious reservations. These were takeovers of what were good, viable operations in Canada that fell into foreign hands, the end result of which was that the viable operations ceased to exist. They were run down and ultimately closed. The end result of that was that the foreign competitor in his own country of origin was able to ship into Canada products that used to be made here because the competitor had successfully worn down the opposition right here in our own country.
I hold no particular torch for FIRA. I do not think that FIRA was a particularly useful mechanism in its over-all capacity to deal with the problem. It is certainly head and shoulders over what we now have before us, and it is for that reason we fought so hard. It is for that reason we took so long. It is for that reason we want to continue the debate on the Investment Canada Bill. It is a vital part of Canada's future.
This debate speaks to what Canada will be ten, fifteen, or twenty years from now. It speaks to whether we will allow almost total foreign ownership of the valuable resources of this land. That is why we are not at all eager to see this Bill dealt with expeditiously.
It is not a question of whether the Government got a mandate on September 4 last. Of course the Government did. However, that mandate did not extend to the dismantling of the very economic structures here. That mandate was more or less given because of the-

It does not. It gives Conservatives the right to be a Government; it gives them the right to bring forward proposals to Parliament. But the parliamentary system is set up in such a way that Government proposes and Parliament disposes. That is what it is all about. The Government brings forward its ideas. It is not as if this change in itself will make it easier. I am suggesting that there are other important matters. There is the whole question of the 1.5 million who remain unemployed notwithstanding the promises of this Government. There is the whole question of the economic direction the country will take as a result of this Government's views on the economy, and since there are serious environmental questions still to be dealt with, and since there are any number of other issues that, combined, made for the reasons people defeated the Liberal Party, why do we not get on and deal with those things? Why must we put in place legislation which has the capacity to undermine the future economy of Canada? Why run the risk of passing a piece of legislation now that would enable the takeovers to take place that until now we have had some serious reservations about? Why pass legislation now to accommodate that, knowing full well what the past history has been and knowing full well that we have, in the main, found it extremely difficult to establish an economic path for Canada when we have had to deal with head offices located in any other part of the world but our own?
The Minister is well aware, I am sure-if he would take off his ideological blinders for a moment and think a little about what has happened in the past-he knows as well as I do of the numerous times when major corporations have made it impossible for their Canadian operations to enter into the world market and to seek out markets for the products they manufacture. He knows of the numbers of times when takeovers have been effected, the cost written off against taxpayers' dollars in Canada, and the company has then closed its doors, become a warehouse for the distribution of products manufactured in some other part of the world, the only purpose of the exercise being to eliminate competition. He knows of the takeovers, using any test one might want to use, that could not be shown to be of any significant benefit to Canada. Recognizing that all of those things have happened in the past and recognizing that as a country we have never been viewed with any great concern, other than for the purpose of monetary return to the investor, by the vast majority of those who would invest in Canada, why would we want to make it easier?
I always think of a conversation I had in Washington. I think it was a Senator who said to me that he did not understand why we were concerned about foreign investment.
I asked him how much foreign investment there is in the United States. It might have been, let us say, 10 per cent of the total number of dollars. It is down about 2 per cent, so I am being generous. It might be around 10 per cent of the total.
I said to him, "Suppose that foreign investment got to 30 per
cent of the total, how would you feel?" He said, "We would never allow it". I said, "Suppose it got to 40 per cent, how would you feel?" "We would never allow it", he said. "It could never happen in the United States". He was telling me that the conditions we have in Canada would be totally unacceptable to the very people who are arguing that they want to impose their conditions on us.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have reached the point in this debate on Bill C-15, which is to kill the Foreign Investment Review Agency, at which the Government has allowed us two hours to conclude debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext: You have been here before.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-15
speechtext:
I have been here before, and I have had the opportunity to speak on the Bill before. I do not want to use all the 10 minutes available because there are many Members on my side who have more they want to say about the Bill. However, I want to make a couple of points.
Before September 4, it was difficult to find members of the Conservative caucus in the House of Commons who believed that closure was ever justified. They were wrong. Closure is sometimes justified. Although they never recognized it in opposition, they certainly recognized quickly in government that closure or time allocation can be a very valuable instrument for the Government to bring the House to a vote on Bills where it is really necessary to deal with them and get on with the public business. I am rising to point out that this is surely not that kind of case. Although the rules permit time allocation now, I think time allocation now is wrong and that the Government has made a mistake in applying it. It has become even more important for us in the Opposition, in the couple of hours we have, to make the point to Canadians that something very valuable will be lost when the Foreign Investment Review Agency is shut down.
For one thing, there is more to be said on the question of foreign investment review. It is a subject in which this country became involved very late. We entered the policy area of foreign investment review long after foreign investment became very far advanced in Canada. While it was largely beneficial to Canada to have the foreign investment we had,
May 21, 1985

while we used it well and we grew as a nation from it, we also paid a higher price than we had to.
I became a Member of Parliament shortly after an intensive review began by the Government of the nature of foreign investment in our country and the question of whether foreign review could be controlled or directed in a way which would still encourage it to come to Canada but in a way that would provide more benefits to Canadians and still be worth-while from the point of view of the foreign investor than had been the case in the past. The Foreign Investment Review Agency was established in that spirit. It is bureaucratic by nature. It is an agency which reviews the plans of business and negotiates with business interests.
Naturally, there may be business interests which would prefer not to have foreign investment review at all. However, on the other hand, any multi-national firm in the world market is aware that almost every country in the world has foreign investment review. Even the United States has it in one way or another. The idea that multi-nationals or others interested in investing in Canada would be deterred by that bureaucratic step was never really proven. I am not satisfied today that any serious business proposition which had wanted to come to Canada would have been deterred by the kind of foreign investment review established by the former Government and in effect in Canada. In fact, if anything, one might have seen a continuation. In fact, there was a continuation of foreign investment in Canada. For all the criticism made of foreign investment review, it appeared to me that most of it was political, most of it was partisan, and most of it was done to design part of the election campaign of the Progressive Conservative Party in the course of the last election.
What has to be remembered in deciding whether the Foreign Investment Review Agency is really the obstacle which the Government says it is is that the Government controls it now. The Foreign Investment Review Agency is an instrument of the Government of the day. It eventually determines whether investments are to be approved. So the argument that we have to proceed here and that we have to collapse this debate because otherwise FIRA will continue inhibiting investment in the country, is wrong on two grounds. It does not inhibit investment and it is controlled by the Government, in effect the final say is at the Cabinet table. On that score the Government is not able to convince the House that any kind of limit, especially the two-hour limit it is seeking to impose on us today, is justified.
A second reason which might be advanced to justify imposing closure today is that this is about the only initiative which the Government has. If we look at virtually all the other legislation on the Order Paper, the other legislation that has gone forward, it is either legislation of a straightforward housekeeping nature or it is legislation that was on the Order Paper when the election was called. I am thinking of all the Bills in the justice area, in particular the one with which I am most familiar. These were initiatives, for the most part, which were well under way when the election was called. The one thing we can say about Bill C-15, the Bill to establish Invest-
Time Allocation
ment Canada, is that it is the legislative program of the Government of Canada today. To my way of thinking that in itself does not justify forcing the Bill through the House any faster than it would be carried by the normal parliamentary process. If the argument is that the Government wants to move forward and put its stamp on the public administration of Canada by bringing forward its first real Bill and getting it enacted in legislation, I do not think it washes as an argument.
I reject it, and I consider on that ground as well that there is no justification for bringing in closure or time allocation to force the House to settle the Bill now.
The third argument which was often used in the past when time allocation was brought forward by former Governments was that there was a heavy legislative backlog, that there was a lot of legislation waiting on the Order Paper to move ahead, and that the Bill before the House, although important, it would be argued, needed to be dealt with so that we could get on with other business. Again, if we look at the Order Paper and at the legislative timetable of the Government, there is nothing else which has to be brought forward on an urgent basis to be considered now. I know our House Leader would be willing to sit down with the Government House Leader, if it were a question of finding time for the rest of the Government's pitifully short legislative program, to permit us to do that according to the Government's timetable and get back to this Bill. I think that kind of agreement could be worked out. On this third ground there is no reason demonstrated for imposing time allocation now. We do not know with what the Government will want to fill the legislative timetable or the time of the House when we have finished consideration of this Bill. In fact, last week and the week before we had something like six days, nearly one after the other, dedicated to opposition business because there was no government legislative business other than this Bill to move forward on. Why can we not give it all the time it requires?
In closing, I want to point out that this is a very important subject. It is not a subject which should be dealt with by time allocation. The way in which foreign investment is to continue in Canada, a country which requires a great deal of foreign investment, is a very important subject, not one which should be wrapped up in the course of a two-hour debate. We should have time to explore all aspects of it. The Government should take the time to try to bring forward the evidence, if there is any other than the anecdotal statements of some businessmen around the world who oppose any kind of government intervention or participation in the activities of an economy. I know the Government can obtain a lot of evidence like that. There are various types of businessmen around who will come forward and say that they would rather not have to deal with Government than deal with Government. However, that is not real proof that the economic development of this country has suffered because of FIRA. We think the case can be made on the other side. The records are there in every FIRA application which went ahead of the kinds of concessions and commitments that were made by foreign investors to ensure that the Canadian economy and the Canadian people would be the

May 21, 1985

clear beneficiaries of every foreign investment made in our country while the Foreign Investment Review Act and the Foreign Investment Review Agency were in place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time, the public has been quite aware of the discussions surrounding FIRA and what would replace it. What the Government was going to do was discussed thoroughly during the election campaign. It was recognized by Canadians that they wanted a change.
Debate on this Bill commenced in the House over five months ago. During that period of time, almost 40 hours of House of Commons time and almost 40 hours of committee time has been used to discuss this Bill, potential amendments to it and the possibility of going back to a form of FIRA. I believe that the time has been well spent but that we have used enough time.
The fact is that unemployment is at a high level, even though it has dropped somewhat. An unemployment rate of 11 per cent is still too high and the need for new jobs and job-creation measures has never been greater. We are looking forward to bringing $100 billion worth of new equity investment to Canada between now and 1991. As this is what is required, it is the target the Government has in mind. Passage of Bill C-15 is one of the steps that will help us bring into this country that new equity that is so badly needed to help create jobs for the many unemployed.
Encouragement of foreign investment can take many forms. It can be a partnership, a joint venture or a minority interest. In changing this climate, we hope that Canadians will once again have renewed confidence in Canada and Canada's future so they too will be encouraged to provide much of that $100 billion worth of new equity which is required.
In Stormont-Dundas, my home riding, there is an unemployment rate of about 15.5 per cent. However, the riding of Stormont-Dundas also has one of the lowest rates of participation in the country, being slightly over 60 per cent. This means that a great number of people have simply given up, are not
looking for work and have lost hope in finding work. Although the published unemployment rate is around 15.5 per cent, if we had a participation rate similar to that of the rest of Canada, the unemployment rate would actually be 21 per cent. If we had a participation rate similar to that of the rest of eastern Ontario, the unemployment rate would be 26 per cent. These figures have been hidden from a public that is very concerned. However, they do emphasize the problems with which we are faced. I am sure that in the near future, not only will we create new jobs but the participation rate will begin to rise as people have more confidence in our ability to create jobs.
Business confidence rose in the first quarter of 1985. The latest Conference Board survey of business attitudes and investment spending intentions indicated the following:
-a growing confidence in Canada's short term economic prospects. An increased proportion of senior managers now see the near-term economic outlook characterized by lower unemployment rates, stronger sales and improved profits. Business confidence in the current investment climate continued to climb following the significant gains registered in the fourth quarter survey.
This confidence is continuing to grow. Passage of Bill C-15 will indicate to the rest of the world that we have confidence in our community, our businesses, our ability to create jobs, and our investment opportunities which are probably the most outstanding investment opportunities available to international investors anywhere in the world.
We recently had the privilege of having a large American company locate in Cornwall with the intention of creating in excess of 200 jobs. We welcome this company. We welcome more Americans, we welcome Europeans and we welcome the entire international investment community. Stormont-Dundas will welcome investors, not only foreign investors but Canadian investors, and it will show some of the negative-minded opposition Members that we can create jobs and we can create them without government intervention.
Perhaps in the next few years we will see the unemployment rate in Stormont-Dundas drop dramatically. I hope and wish that members of the Opposition will join me in a positive thrust to create new jobs. Get behind the people who are unemployed. Rather than pushing them down, help lift them up. We have a new era ahead. I invite all Hon. Members to join us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hundreds of thousands of people, indeed millions of people from industrialized countries like the United States, Canada, Great Britain, Germany, France, Belgium and Holland have lost their jobs in recent years. They have lost their jobs partly because of the development of new technology requiring fewer workers and partly because the new technologies are being exported to formerly under-developed countries like South Korea and Brazil where the most modern manufacturing plants are being set up. These plants are producing the manufactured goods which in the past were produced in industrialized countries while paying workers a fraction of what workers from the industrialized countries formerly made.
Workers in this country are facing the same problems as workers in other industrialized countries. However, our situa-
May 21, 1985

tion, is probably worse than that of workers in other countries because so much of Canada's manufacturing industry is owned and controlled by companies with head offices and owners located in other countries. These head offices and owners are located mainly in the United States, but there are also some in Japan, Germany and Great Britain.
When foreign-based companies make decisions, those decisions will not necessarily be made taking into account what is good for Canada and Canadian workers. Very often, decisions will be made taking into account what is good for shareholders and management, and also because of pressure that is put on these companies by their Governments. Why should that not be so? Why should the American Government not be concerned about the unemployment rate in the United States? Why should it not be putting pressure on multi-national corporations to create as many jobs as possible in that country rather than in Canada?
There is another problem which we face. Every day of the week we are being told by business leaders, by Government and by academics that in order to survive and to provide jobs, we must be more efficient and productive and that to do that, we must put more effort into research and development. We know about Canada's record in research and development. We know that of all of the OECD countries including countries in western Europe and the countries of the United States and Japan, Canada is at the bottom of the list when it comes to the effort we put into research and development. When other countries are spending 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent, sometimes more, of their GNP on research and development, we are spending half of that. The Conservatives, in their run-up to the election, promised that by 1990 we would be spending 2.5 per cent of our GNP on research and development. But we know what has happened. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon), has made it very clear that we are not going to reach that figure because the Government has to cut back. We also know that among the worst offenders, the companies which spend the least on research and development, are the multi-nationals.
I do not know if what I am going to illustrate today is still a fact, but I know that several years ago Ford Motor Company, which was doing about $500 million worth of business here a year, did not have a single Ph.D. graduate working on research in this country. That is the situation and that is why we believe and have believed for many years that it is important that as much of our industry as possible should be Canadian-owned. The Government, working with those industries, could then ensure that they develop policies and follow objectives that were good for Canada and Canadian workers. That is why we were so insistent when the Liberals were in power that we get legislation which would encourage Canadian ownership. That is why we kept the pressure on the former Liberal Government to pass legislation establishing FIRA. As so often has happened with Liberal Governments, it took steps to give the appearance that it was doing something when in fact it had no real intention of seeing that real steps are taken. So we have
Time Allocation
the situation where, particularly in the last few years, 95 per cent or more of all the applications to FIRA by multi-national companies to take over Canadian companies were approved. So that FIRA became something which was to a large extent ignored. It really did not work.
We have always believed that the Government of Canada has to protect the people of Canada. It has to see that the industrial development which takes place in this country is of benefit not just to the shareholders but to the Canadian people. That is why we have opposed the present Government's proposal to do away with FIRA and replace it with Investment Canada.
Let me give just a couple of illustrations of the kind of thing we believe could very well happen if we did away with the present legislation and opened the doors to any foreign company that wanted to come in. The Government now owns two of the largest aerospace companies in this country, namely, de Havilland, which has its main operations in Toronto, and Canadair, with its main operations in Montreal. These two companies employ thousands of workers. How is it that they are now Crown corporations? After all, originally, and for many years, they were privately owned. I want Members on the Government side to remember that it was not some socialist Government which believed in public ownership of everything which took those companies over. What happened was that, as in many countries, the aerospace industry was going through a period of recession and the private owners of those two companies said they could not continue, they were losing too much money, and they were ready to close down. The former Liberal Government of Canada said that every industrialized country in the world has an aerospace industry, that Some of the most important inventions used in all kinds of industry were made originally in the aerospace industry, so it cannot let the aerospace industry disappear. If the private sector will not continue to operate Canadair and de Havilland, then the Government of Canada, on behalf of the people of Canada, is going to take these two companies over.
Now I am not going to defend the way in which those companies were managed, but I certainly believe, and 1 think the people of Canada believe, that we need to have an aerospace industry in this country. The Government now proposes to privatize those two companies. It may be that they could be privatized by virtually giving them away, but I hope that not even a Conservative Government would do that. However, it may be that right now the aerospace industry world-wide is on an upturn and they can be sold at a fair price. But I ask the Minister, what if four or five years down the road the industry is again in brouble and the new owners want to sell these companies? Will the Government let the aerospace industry disappear, or will we again go through the process of taking them over?
This makes no sense to us, and that is why we believe this legislation is wrong. That is why we believe the Government of Canada has to have the power and authority to be involved in the decision-making concerning what happens in the continu-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the motion before this House because it is obvious that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) is really on a power trip. He obviously wants to get rid of the Foreign Investment Review Act and get all the power in his own hands in order to deal with the few applications which will come to the Government for review. I suppose he wants to do that because he has really had a dismal record of bringing new investment into this country in the six or eight months he has been the Minister.
Let us look back to the time just a year ago to the situation when the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, during a period of about three months, announced something like $2 billion worth of new automobile plant construction in Ontario alone. I will recite the list of plants created because we tend to forget these things. We listen to the Mulroney malar-key and to what the present Minister has to say, but we forget that they have not really been able to bring in any major new automobile assembly or parts manufacturing plants. Looking back we see that a Honda plant, worth $100 million, creating 350 jobs, was approved. Then there was the AMC Renault assembly and parts manufacturing plant, worth some $700 million, going into Brampton, with 7,000 jobs being created. There is also a General Motors steel production and parts plant in Oshawa that is worth $1 billion. There is another General Motors plant in St. Catharines which manufactures engines that is worth $255 million. Those plants amount to over $2 billion and represent some 10,000 jobs. We only have to look at press clippings since that time to realize that the Minister, who talked about bringing in more automobile assembly plants in the fall, has not accomplished very much in that regard. Obviously, the Minister wants to have all the power, for whatever reviews there will be, in his own hands. He does not even want to have to refer them to Cabinet. We could look back at the number of applications which went before FIRA. In 1983, there were 860 applications which did not require review. If applications under Investment Canada are to take over a Canadian company, is the company going to be shut down? Will they also take over the sales force and lay off people? Those are the concerns which many Canadians have with respect to Investment Canada.
On this side of the House we find it incomprehensible that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), before he met with the press and before coming to the House, ran to the United States and made the commitment to do away with FIRA without holding negotiations. Surely, even the Tories agree that it is very useful to have a Foreign Investment Review Act, when new funds are coming into the country or foreigners propose to take over a Canadian company, to be able to negotiate and to ensure that the jobs will be kept, the plant will continue to run, that research will be done in Canada, and that a reasonable
share of the international market will be maintained for Canada.
The American foreign control legislation is just as extensive as ours, however , the United States does not have a one-stop shopping situation such as FIRA. People wanting to invest in the United States are required to comb through a whole list of frederal and state legislation. Federal legislation in the United States has 17 Acts which restrict foreign investment. Six of those Acts provide restrictions as to who can invest and participate. Eight of those Acts provide a total prohibition of ownership. The legislation covers many fields. For example, coastal and fresh water shipping is totally prohibited under The Jones Act and the Merchant Marine Act. Dredging and salvage operations are restricted under the Regulation of Vessels in Domestic Commerce legislation. Shipbuilding is barred from government benefit programs under the Fishing Fleet Improvement Act, the Merchant Marine Act and the Merchant Ship Sales Act. In the fishing area, countries which have reciprocal agreements are restricted, and others are prohibited, under the Fish and Wildlife Act and the Fishery Conservation and Management Act. There is a long list of legislation concerning restrictions and prohibitions which cover activities such as those of domestic air carriers in which investment is prohibited under the Federal Aviation Act. International air carriers are restricted under the International Air Transportation Fair Competitive Practices Act. Activities such as radio, television, telegraph and telephone licensing are prohibited under the Communications Act. Radio and television operators are prohibited under the Communications Act. In addition, nuclear power is prohibited under the Atomic Energy Act. Hydroelectric facilities are restricted under the Federal Power Act. The transmission of natural gas and electricity are permitted or restrained under the Federal Power Act. Yet the attitude of the Tories is that Canadian ownership is not necessary or desirable.
I think Canadians believe that Canadian ownership is desirable. In fact, during the first three years of the National Energy Program, Canadian ownership rose from 28 per cent to 40 per cent. That is an amazing performance for a three-year period. During that same period of time we increased our reserves in natural gas to a 33-year horizon and arranged for reserves of oil which will last until the end of the century. Yet the transmission of natural gas and electricity is on the list of American restrictions and prohibitions.
I would like to continue dealing with U.S. legislation. The transfer of federally-owned lands is prohibited unless it is by reciprocal agreement under the Small Tract Act. Mineral rights, such as to oil and coal, are prohibited, unless there is a reciprocal agreement, under the Mineral Land Leasing Act. In addition, the mineral leases on the continental shelf, which include oil, gas and sulphur, are restricted, and in practice are prohibited, under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
The Americans have a whole list of restrictions and prohibitions which the Tories want to throw wide open in Canada. If the Government is to bring in an Investment Canada Bill, we cannot understand why the Prime Minister and the President
May 21, 1985

did not sit down to negotiate. Instead of throwing Canada wide open with no restrictions on investments under $5 million, we might have negotiated away some of the restrictions concerning Canadian ownership in the United States.
I believe the Tories are putting a hammer to our heads by forcing the vote today on Investment Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to make representations here, as well as in writing, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on behalf of pensioners and , senior citizens who | receive lumpsum pension payments.
I am referring to lumpsum payments made either under the Canada Pension Plan or by foreign Governments with which

May 21, 1985
we have international agreements, when an application usually requires several years before it is processed and concluded.
1 urge the Minister to consider the merits of introducing a measure in the Budget permitting pensioners who receive a lumpsum payment to average it over the number of years for which the payment is being made.
