Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that on this day when the International Conference on Human Rights is resuming in Ottawa there is a disturbing development in the case of the world famous Soviet dissident, Andrei Sakharov. Attempts by his step-daughter in the United States or reach Dr. Sakharov have proved unsuccessful today. There are suggestions that this internationally known dissident has resumed a hunger strike over the denial to his wife, Yelena Bonner, of permission to receive medical treatment in the West for her serious heart condition, treatment not available to her in the Soviet Union.
It is shocking in this age of instant communication that a simple telephone call between a relative and an international figure famous for his scholarship and human rights activities is impossible to arrange. Therefore I ask the Government to make immediate representations to the Soviet Government, first, to permit Mrs. Bonner to leave the Soviet Union to receive treatment that is not available in the U.S.S.R.; second, to permit the family to establish contact with relatives in the United States; third, to permit representatives of western Governments or the news media to visit Gorky, which is a closed city, in order that Dr. Sakharov's many supporters throughout the world can be informed of his condition.
I am sure that this statement has the support of all Members in the House, and that the Government will act promptly in expressing Canadian concerns.

maintopic: VETERANS' VISIT TO THE NETHERLANDS AND ITALY
VETERANS' VISIT TO THE NETHERLANDS AND ITALY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this month thousands of Canadian veterans returned to the battle zones of the Second World War to attend the 40th anniversary of the liberation of the Netherlands and of Italy where the Canadian Forces played a major role in driving out the Nazis. For a few days the veterans relived the horrors of war and vividly recalled the fatigue, the hunger, the thirst, the noise, and the agony of seeing their comrades die as they climbed the mountains and crossed the rivers under heavy gunfire. The Canadians could not be stopped, for they fought for the freedom of the people and for the sovereignty of the nations.
Typically, as in other places, in Wageningen where the Nazis unconditionally surrendered to the Canadians, thousands of people of all ages lined the streets and cheered the veterans as they marched; hundreds put out their hands to touch a veteran while shouting "Thank you, Canada!"
During the impressive commemorative services held in the war cemeteries where the bodies of Canadians lie beneath grave stones carrying the Maple Leaf, wreaths were reverently laid, and while the R.C.N. Brass Band and Bagpipes beautifully rendered "Amazing Grace", hundreds meditated and prayed. In front of the grave of a 21-year old Canadian, a lady with her family exclaimed: "Thank you . .. because of your sacrifice we are free!" And they all bowed their heads and thanked God for the Canadians who cared enough to offer their lives, and even to die, so others could be free and so their nation could be sovereign. Holland and Italy say, "Thank you, Canada".

Mr. Speaker, a new coalition has formed in Canada to disseminate inaccurate, alarmist propaganda. Known as the Toronto Disarmament Network, this left wing advertising co-operative has drawn together an interesting group of infamous Canadians.
In a full page newspaper advertisement published yesterday, this group attempts to convince Canadians that the U.S. Strategic Defence Initiative Research Project will somehow make Canada less secure. In fact Canadians know that this is a gross misstatement.
But one only need to consider where this inaccurate propaganda originates. The group that signed this particular misleading ad includes none other than the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and 15 of his caucus colleagues; the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), and his fellow Liberal, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia); the Communist Party of Canada; the Karl Marx Club of Winnipeg, and the Young Communist League of Toronto, to name just a few. It is interesting to see this polarization of like minded people.

Mr. Speaker, our Canadian national soccer team is doing extremely well in its march to next year's World Cup finals in Mexico City. The team has fielded a young, dynamic, and able selection of Canadian
May 21, 1985

talent. All Canadians take pride in these sports' ambassadors, and all wish them well on the international sports scene.
However, a projected deficit of close to $500,000 is seriously plaguing their efforts. In response, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) has committed total and full support, but no money. This kind of action will not score any goals with anyone.
The team needs more than words of encouragement. This year alone over $600,000 of federal money was provided to the Canadian Sports Association, but because of some unrealistic, outdated restrictions, not a single penny reached the national team. I urge the Minister to remove these impediments immediately so that this and other national teams may receive the financial assistance they rightfully deserve.
In addition, the Minister, in typical fashion, has passed the buck to the private sector. However, the corporate sector has already committed more than $1 million in sponsorship for the team.
It is clear that it is the Minister who must now act, and toward this end I challenge him and the Government, from today on, to match any private or corporate donations to our national soccer team. This would show leadership and commitment, and offer an incentive that would be responsed by those very Canadians whom the Minister is asking for financial help.

Mr. Speaker, in the recently released annual report of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association, the lack of the Conservative Government's commitment to the Canadian shipbuilding industry is evident. It is clear that the Canadian shipbuilding industry is in need of government attention.
Government statistics show that the number of people employed by the industry has decreased rapidly over the past few years. In 1982, 12,000 were employed in the Canadian shipyards. In 1984, the number is down to 7,000.
At the same time there was a dramatic increase in the number of foreign built vessels registered in Canada. Canadian ship transport companies are going offshore to purchase their vessels, and Canadian workers in the industry are suffering from the Government's inaction.
The Conservative promises to the industry appear to have been forgotten. Where is the extension of concessionary financing terms to Canadian customers of Canadian shipyards? Foreign customers can already obtain such terms through the Export Development branch.
Where are the incentives to increase the Canadian content in vessels used to export Canadian natural resources? Where is the promised doubling of the rate of duty for the temporary importation of foreign vessels when no suitable Canadian vessels are available?
These and other promises were made by the present Government. Instead, the Government has cancelled the SIAP Program and has left the industry to fend for itself. The Canadian shipbuilding industry is hopefully awaiting the Conservative's Budget. However, given the Government's past inaction, we on this side of the House believe that it will be sorely disappointed.

subtopic: LIFE MAGAZINE'S SLIGHTING OF CANADIAN WORLD WAR II VETERANS
LIFE MAGAZINE'S SLIGHTING OF CANADIAN WORLD WAR II VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my outrage and indignation over an unconscionable slight to Canada and Canadians by our neighbours to the South.
A special 114-page issue of Life Magazine features stories and pictures about the heroes and battles of World War II, highlighting veterans from the United States and most, if not all, of our other Allies. The magazine had enough space for a section highlighting heroes from Germany and Japan, but apparently not enough space even to mention Canada's part, which is said by others to be a greater part per capita than any other Allied country. It was a valiant and heroic role which is well remembered and honoured in Europe.
As a veteran, I had the honour this month to be a member of the Canadian delegation which travelled to the Netherlands and Italy to commemorate the fortieth anniversary of VE Day. Our delegation, composed of many distinguished veterans, including a recipient of the Victoria Cross, visited more than 20 war cemeteries where more than 10,000 Canadian war dead are buried. In both the Netherlands and Italy we participated in ceremonies organized by their respective Governments to pay tribute to Canada and to the Canadians who liberated their countries 40 years ago, and to the thousands of Canadians who gave their lives in doing so.
That a major American publication can obliterate Canada's important role in World War II, by failing to acknowledge our presence, is an inexcusable omission.

maintopic: OIL PRICES-POSITION ADVANCED BY MULTINATIONAL COMPANIES
OIL PRICES-POSITION ADVANCED BY MULTINATIONAL COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to tell the people of Canada that the Government has been had. The Government gave into the demands of the multinationals in exchange for new investment, but the Government is coming up short.
Three of the five major multinationals have said that even with the money that has been given to them by the Government, they want more. Gulf Canada President Keith McWal-ter says: "Higher real crude oil prices will be required in the 1990s to warrant the development of new supply sources". Mr. Speaker, last week one of the most successful federal and provincial conferences ever was held in Winnipeg. I refer to the federal-provincial conference on multiculturalism. The House resumed from Friday, May 17, 1985 consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski (for the Minister of Agriculture) that Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to have the opportunity this afternoon to speak on Bill C-25 and to comment on the remarks made by the distinguished Parliamentary Secretary last Friday when he introduced the Bill in the House.
Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act, is clearly a very important piece of legislation. It was first introduced about one year ago as Bill C-50. I am not sure why the Government has taken so long to introduce it in the House. There is a great deal of concern in the red meat industry about the current difficulties and problems faced by that industry.
We are pleased that the Bill is now before the House. The purpose of the Bill is to provide a stabilization program for red meat under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. It is a tripartite red meat stabilization program in which the provinces, the producers and the federal Government jointly and equally participate in the establishment of a uniform stabilization program. This would prevent top loading by some provinces because many provinces already have their own stabilization program.
The provincial stabilization programs have caused some concern in the country because the United States has imposed a countervail on pork and hogs going into the United States.

May 21, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
Therefore, one of the objectives of this program should be to establish and provide funds for a uniform tripartite red meat stabilization program. In fact, five funds will be established in this regard, one for cow-calf operators, one for backgrounder cattle; one for slaughtering cattle, one for hogs, and one for sheep operations.
The Bill provides that the three participants would share equally in the funding of the program and the Government's contribution would not exceed 6 per cent of the gross receipts of the participating producers.
A number of changes were made to the Bill that was originally introduced in the House in January. These changes, which would be retroactive to January 1, provide that stabilization could take place for less than a one-year period as provided in the former legislation. The price support formula for stabilization programs would be different from the one in the existing legislation. It provides for the establishment of a fund within the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the federal Government.
The greatest difficulty facing the Government with respect to this legislation is the problem of whether it will get full participation from the red meat sector. Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario have indicated their willingness to participate, and this represents a very significant proportion in terms of the total share of the production of red meat. With respect to slaughtered cattle, it represents approximately 94 per cent; approximately 88 per cent with respect to cow-calf production; 94 per cent for backgrounders; 79 per cent for lambs; and 57 per cent for hogs.
The question remains whether British Columbia, Quebec and the three Maritime Provinces will participate. Unless they support this legislation it is questionable if it will meet the objectives of preventing the balkanization of the Canadian production and market-place for red meat which seems to be taking place under current circumstances.
Last summer, the federal Government was very careful not to provide stabilization for the number of hogs that were sold into the Canadian market. Clearly, we do not want to contravene our GATT requirements in the American market-place because stabilization of production going into the international trade subjects us to countervails. That is the reason for a countervailing duty on pork production in Canada and the investigation which is taking place by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
This legislation will establish a national program which could take into account some of the production of red meat that goes into the United States and other markets in order to prevent the contravention of our GATT commitments.
Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary could indicate this afternoon how much progress has been made in getting the co-operation of the other provinces that have yet to join the program. Unless the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) is willing to work out the details necessary for negotiation with those other provinces, the program will not be as effective and desirable as we would like.
That uncertainty is apparent in a Canadian Press story dated May 8. The Minister of Agriculture from Alberta expressed his concern about the proposal and his wish that the proposal not be changed if his province is to participate. He also expressed concern that many beef producers in this country believe that the federal Government has sold them out by increasing the quotas to the European Economic Community countries. The House will recall that in September, quotas were set at some 5.9 million pounds for 1985. It certainly appears that the Government will increase that quota to over 20 million pounds. That will have a devastating impact on the industry. I am sure it prompted the Minister of Agriculture in Alberta, as reported in the Canadian Press story on May 8, to say;
We keep getting traded off in agriculture all the time. We have import levels of meat coming into this country. We don't mind competing with them, as long as it's not subsidized.
I suggest that that underscores the concern in the industry as a result of those increases in beef quotas from the European Economic Community.
The purpose of this Bill is not to provide a continual production subsidy but, rather, to provide assistance when the price drops dramatically. The price of pork has dropped dramatically in the last few weeks as a result of the countervail imposed by the United States. That countervail will remain until late July, at which time we will know if it will be imposed for a full year.
This legislation will be very beneficial in eliminating the wide fluctuation in prices for red meat. It is clearly not a marketing tool in itself because it is not designed to provide a market for red meat commodities. It is designed to provide stabilization when there are dramatic drops in price. I think in that regard it will be interesting in the committee hearings to hear the details of how the legislation will work. The Committee on Agriculture must find out exactly which provinces are prepared to participate in the program, because otherwise we will end up with a very balkanized situation in the production of red meat, with Quebec having a massive program of stabilization payments, some of the Maritime provinces having a very rich program, whereas many of the other provinces, the ones that have indicated they want to participate, not having similar type legislation and assistance available.
Those are some of the concerns that I have with the legislation. I hope the Minister will be successful in getting all the provinces to participate. I hope that we will be able to get a clear indication of support and participation from those other provinces. Clearly, the red meat industry today is probably in one of the most desperate situations we have seen in many years, not only because of the continuing level of low commodity prices, but because of high interest rates and, as we have seen, the dramatic drop in the last couple of years in the value of land, which has wiped out the equity many young producers have in their farms. All of those things, combined with the continuing increase in input costs, plus the countervail
May 21, 1985

that we have seen put on pork and hogs during the last couple of months, have had a devastating impact.
That is the reason for the dramatic report last fall of the Farm Credit Corporation which indicated that a large percentage, over 17 per cent, of our farm operators, especially the young ones, are facing serious financial difficulty. The situation has worsened since then with a drop in prices of pork and hogs by some $10 or $12 per animal. We have seen the increase in the European Economic Community quota which the industry has already recognized even though the Government has not made a formal announcement of that massive increase, but all in all it makes for a very difficult situation, one which requires government action.
I hope that besides working this legislation through the committee, improving it and making it functional, we will look at other ways to assist the red meat industry. I hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), on Thursday night when he stands in his place to deliver his Budget speech, will adopt at least some of the recommendations, hopefully all of the recommendations, of the Finance Committee which recommended, I believe, a $96 million agri-bond program, which is designed to assist some of the 39,000 young farmers who are facing very serious financial difficulties. Many of them will lose their farms this season.
Last week I was in Alberta. I was talking to one of the people responsible for the Alberta Agriculture Development Corporation. He indicated that many of the young farmers who have been in production for only a few years have a large capital debt, and with the reduction in the price of hogs brought about by the countervail they are facing a very short time period in which to recover their financial stability. In his opinion they will be facing the loss of their farms within a period of two or three months.
This legislation, within its limited scope, can be beneficial to the agricultural community. It is essentially the same Bill as the one introduced last June by Mr. Whelan when he was the Minister of Agriculture. I hope the Bill will move on to the standing committee where we can call witnesses with a view to making the Bill as functional and as beneficial as we can. Hopefully, the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to indicate to us this afternoon how much success there has been in getting the support and assistance of the other four or five provinces which have not until now indicated they would be willing to participate in this legislation.
1 hope the Bill will go to committee in the next couple of days and that we will be able to go on with more detailed study at that time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that last September 4 representations were being made by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association to trigger the meat import law. It took the Government three months to trigger that meat import law. By that time we had actually gone beyond the allotted 145 million pounds. Had the law been triggered on or about October 1, we would not have gone beyond the 145 million pounds, which is the historical guaranteed minimum access level. Finally, belatedly, after three months in power the Government did trigger the meat import law. It restricted the United States to 21 million pounds. The Government restricted the EEC, especially Ireland and Denmark, to 5.9 million pounds and Nicaragua to 600,000 pounds of meat. Other countries, such as Australia and New Zealand, were restricted to more traditional amounts. It is with great chagrin and concern that a few weeks after the Government established the quotas for the 1985 period we learned what the Government had done. It had secretly negotiated with the United States to increase its quotas from 21 million pounds to what I understand will be 65 million pounds. Also we heard that negotiations were under way for Nicaragua to increase its quotas from some 600,000 pounds to close to nine million pounds, and it may even be higher. There is as well the question of the United States embargo which was imposed recently. With regard to the EEC, we do not know exactly what it will come down to, but we understand that it will be 23.5 million pounds.
I asked the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) why he and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), when they were in Europe a few weeks ago, did not take this matter up with the heads of Governments-with the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Presidents of France and Italy, and the Chancellor of West Germany. If they were unable to raise it together, they could have done it on a bilateral basis as it was an important question. The Minister for International Trade indicated that there was not time or there was not concern on the part of the Government to maintain the quotas imposed under our meat import law.
I am aware of the import levels. I am aware that the Government triggered the meat import law on December 21 but did not have the intestinal fortitude to stand up to the EEC. As a result, we have not only an increase of some 17 million pounds of beef coming into the country, which works out to about 1,000 carcasses per week of additional meat coming to the market at a time when commodity prices are

May 21, 1985

low, but we have also upset the Australians, our traditional trading partners. They are very concerned about an additional 1,000 carcasses a week coming to the Canadian market of subsidized beef at 48 cents per pound, subsidized by the Treasuries of European countries. Australian is very concerned because it has had an historical access of a very large amount of beef, lower quality cuts. This is very harmful to our agricultural community.
I hope the Hon. Member will be able to make strong representations in caucus to the Minister for International Trade and to the Minister of Agriculture as I have been making in the House since January when it became apparent that the Government was planning to cave in to the pressures and threats of the countervails which the EEC was putting on the Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those are the kinds of questions which we will certainly want to delve into in committee. The Bill contains certain conditions about the amount of commitment that Governments can make. I think it is 6 per cent of the gross receipts for individual commodities. Also the fund must have fiscal integrity. In other words, it is not as if the Government would bail out the fund or producers would have to put more into it. We clearly have a serious problem in the red meat industry. We certainly want to save the industry. We want to see it continue to function. Certainly the formula will be one of the things we will want to examine in committee.
I know of the concern of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) in this regard. I would like to look at those aspects of the Bill at committee stage. As I said earlier, I do not believe it is possible under this legislation to solve many of the farm debt problems. They will have to be dealt with in the Budget on Thursday night. I hope the Minister of Finance will do that.
My other concern at this stage is how we get hog and beef producers to pay their premium with the industry being in such a devastated position this year. That is another matter we will want to consider in committee. I have had hog producers telephoning me and saying that they hoped this legislation would be in position immediately. Certainly we want to expedite it, but I am not sure that it can be moved forward rapidly enough to have pay-outs or even that the formula would trigger pay-outs over a short period of time, given the depressed state of the industry right now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on Bill C-25. I represent a mixed
community of urban and rural people. In fact, in the rural sector I represent a fair number of hog and beef producers. One does not have to represent rural areas to know that there is a severe crisis in agriculture today. Canadian farmers face a very uncertain future. If they look back over the last few years, they see that the prices for their commodities have either fallen or else have not kept up with the ever increasing cost of production. The squeeze in which they find themselves is forcing many people off the farms and is creating real stumbling blocks for young people to get into farming.
We have only to look at the statistics to know how serious the situation is. For example, in 1979 there were 125 farm bankruptcies in Canada. In 1980, there were 222; in 1981, there were 261; in 1982, there were 410; in 1983, there were 488; and in 1984, there were 551. Every year for the last number of years the number of farm bankruptcies has increased, and that is only the tip of the iceberg. In 1979, the estimated farm debt outstanding from all sources-that is, short, intermediate and long-term-was $14.6 billion, carrying an average interest rate of some 11.6 per cent. In 1981, the outstanding farm debt increased to $18.5 billion at an average interest rate of 15.46 per cent. In 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation reported in its survey that outstanding farm debts amounted to $20.7 billion, with an interest rate well in the two digit level.
We can look at some of the other problems. For example, in its 1984 farm survey report, the Farm Credit Corporation shows that one in five of a total of 37,000 Canadian farmers are in serious financial trouble with debt costs exceeding 40 per cent of income. There were 551 farmers who declared bankruptcy in 1984, a 20 per cent increase over 1983. The FCC estimates that another 1,700 farmers are on the brink of immediate insolvency.
We know that the situation is becoming much more difficult, particularly for the younger farmers. The younger section of the farm community has the weakest equity position and is most vulnerable to escalating interest costs and hence to foreclosure and liquidation. Unless decisive action is taken, Canada stands to lose a whole generation of its most efficient and productive farmers.
The FCC report went on to indicate that one-third of the farms carried about 80 per cent of the $20.7 million in outstanding farm debt and that about half the food produced annually in Canada came from these farms. In other words, of a total agricultural debt of some $20.7 billion, 80 per cent of it was carried by those farmers who produce about half of Canada's annual farm produce. Therefore, lack of productivity is not at issue, but income certainly is.
Let us take a look at income. Net farm income in 1984 is no higher in actual dollar terms than it was in 1974, and has fallen by a staggering 30 per cent in real terms over the past four years alone. We have a case of increasing costs and decreasing prices. It certainly does not require an economist or a farmer to realize that we cannot continue operating under
May 21, 1985

these conditions for too long. As the figures demonstrate, more and more farmers are being squeezed off the land. They no longer find what their parents and very often their grandparents did to be a productive activity.
The crisis in agriculture is not merely an economic question. Surely it is also a social question. Can we as a country afford to lose our agricultural sector? Can we afford to see ever-increasing numbers of farmers go into bankruptcy? What are the social implications of this? Surely a reasonable minded person would find that this situation is unacceptable and that our agricultural community must be kept viable.
We have to maintain the part of this country that is inhabited by farmers. Statistics indicate that there are fewer and fewer family farms and that these family farms will be replaced more and more often by large corporate farms. That,
I believe, we all find unacceptable, regardless of political Party. I think we are all committed to maintaining the family farm as a viable economic unit and we all recognize that it is in the best interests of this country to maintain a viable agricultural community. For agriculture to be taken over by large corporate agri-business is not socially desirable. In fact, it will essentially lead to a new type of feudalism. In feudal times, feudal lords owned and controlled large tracts of land and the people who worked the soil were in essence the peasants or salaried agricultural workers, not the people who owned the land.
We must all recognize the seriousness of the problem that faces this country. This problem is not one that is faced by farmers alone; it is a problem that must concern us all. If we do not have a viable, healthy agricultural sector, everyone in the country will suffer. When farmers in Saskatchewan do poorly, the people of my riding of Regina East do poorly. The small shopkeepers and manufacturing and service centres that service the agricultural community do poorly. That means that there are more layoffs and less economic activity in Regina. The entire city and the entire province suffer. The same is true for Ontario, Quebec and other industrial areas. If farmers do poorly, farm implement companies cannot sell their products and they in turn must lay off workers. Manufacturing, servicing, retailing and wholesaling interests in Ontario, Quebec and the larger industrial regions suffer. The wellbeing of our agricultural sector is important to all men and women across this country.
What we are facing today is not simply a farm crisis, but a national crisis. It is a national crisis that must be addressed. Unfortunately, there is very little in Bill C-25 to address the issue. The Conservative Government has done very little so far to indicate that it recognizes the seriousness of the problem and that is capable of doing something about it. Despite the promises that we heard made during the election campaign, we have not seen much action.
During the election campaign, we heard Conservative Members denounce years of Liberal inaction, and promises to safeguard the future of the independent family farm. More specifically, we were told that a Progressive Conservative Government would establish a farm finance review board to
Agricultural Stabilization Act
adjust farm debts. At that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) told the Empire Club and the Canadian Club that new expenditures of $100 million would be made available in 1985-86 for farm mortgage financing. We heard many good promises being made last summer. It is too had that we have not seen them put into action since the summer. It is too bad that we are not seeing legislative action being taken today on the promises made by the Conservative Party during the election campaign.
Government Members have certainly had plenty of time to bring forward measures that would help strengthen the farm economy. Instead, we have Bill C-25. As everyone admits, it is essentially the same as the Whelan Bill, Bill C-50, which was introduced almost a year ago. It does nothing to solve the basic problem facing agriculture. It provides for stabilization based on market returns, but that will be insensitive to future cost increases. It will do nothing to raise price and net farm incomes. It is lacking because it does not offer a stabilization program that actually meets or begins to meet the real costs that farmers must face in order to produce red meat products.
By averaging out market returns over time, the Bill does take a very small step forward. However, that step is inadequate when the market itself has failed to generate a return to the farmer which covers his or her costs of production and a reasonable return on capital and labour. It is a stabilization plan based on prices which have been in effect for the last number of years. Those prices are inadequate in meeting the real costs of production. What we have is stabilization based on unacceptable prices.
We have been urging the Government to recognize that there is a need for a cost-based insurance system or a stabilization program. It is that type of program which we wish the Government would introduce. We want a program which is based on the real cost of production one which will ensure our farmers a sensible rate of return on their capital and labour investments in order that Canadian farmers and producers can carry out their important functions with a sense that there is a Government and a nation which cares enough to ensure that they will get an adequate rate of return on what they produce.
It is not an outrageous proposal. Everyone recognizes that agriculture in Canada is the least subsidized when compared to any other part of the world. American agriculture is subsidized through a variety of programs. The European Economic Community subsidizes its farmers in all sorts of different ways. Canadian farmers are the most efficient in the world, but faced with subsidized foreign competition, our farmers do not stand a chance. They stand a chance if they compete on a one-to-one basis with a farmer or a cattle producer in Ireland, France, Germany, Iowa or any other part of the world, but they do not stand a chance if they are competing against a farmer whose Government is standing behind him. Is it not time for us to stop expecting Canadian farmers to stand naked and alone in the world when competing against farmers in other parts of the world who have their respective Govern-

May 21, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
ments standing behind them? Is it not time to begin to guarantee to farmers in Canada a fair rate of return on their activity? It is not that the farmers are asking much; they are only asking for a fair rate of return.
Farmers do not have the clout which other players in the economy have. If a manufacturer of goods and services discovers that his costs have increased, he is able to jack up the price and recover the increase in his costs. When banks have to pay more interest to attract savers, they charge higher interest rates to the borrowers. Many working people in the organized trade union movement are able to recover increases in their cost of living the next time they bargain and achieve a wage settlement. However, I must say that the trade unions have been losing their clout over the last number of years. In fact, actual wages have declined as a percentage of the increase in the cost of living. Working people are discovering a reduction in their standard of living something farmers have been experiencing for a number of years. Farmers cannot pass on their cost of production increases. Therefore, farmers depend upon a collective action, whether it be a marketing board or a collective action taken by the federal and provincial Governments. Otherwise, farmers do not stand a chance in Hades of surviving.
I am certain that the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), who has a number of cattlemen in his riding, understands that. Even though he is a free enterpriser, I am sure he will admit that as far as agricultural production in Canada is concerned, there are limits to the free market. Given what Governments are doing in other parts of the world, there is a need for some collective action.
We believe that Bill C-25 is inadequate. It does not deal with the basic problem which farmers face. Neither does it deal with the whole question of front-end loading. The Province of British Columbia, the Province of Quebec and the Maritimes have offered certain forms of subsidies. The Provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario do not provide subsidies and object to front-end loading. The present legislation will not help producers in British Columbia, Quebec and the Maritimes. That is not entirely fair. The Province of Alberta has what could be called "bottom-end loading". The cost of production in Alberta might not be the same as in other provinces because Alberta does not charge a tax on gasoline.
A co-operative approach is needed. Ministers of Agriculture and producers from across Canada should sit down with the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to discuss these matters. A system should be established across Canada to eliminate the possibility of price wars between provinces. What we need first and foremost is leadership from the Government and the Minister of Agriculture. We have not seen that leadership, therefore the farm crisis in Canada will get worse and worse. Until we have leadership, Bill C-25 will not provide a solution.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made a brief reference to interest rates without elaborating very much. I think one of the very big problems farmers are having right now are high interest rates. I spoke in the House on Friday and read off the increase in bankruptcies of farmers over the last four or Five years. It has gone up by leaps and bounds. One of the major problems in this country is the fact that we need to bring down interest rates. This was promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was campaigning as Leader of the Conservative Party, and it seems to me we should be doing more about that. I would like to ask the Hon. Member what ideas he has for bringing down interest rates in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, historically interest rates have generally been around two points above the inflation rate. We now have an inflation rate of around 3 per cent or 4 per cent. I am willing to give them 7 per cent, three points above the inflation rate. At 7 per cent, a lot of economic activity in this country all at once becomes viable. A lot of farm activity and small business activity all at once becomes viable. It becomes viable to think about putting out some money on a new home.
One of the central problems we have to address ourselves to is that of interest rates. I could stand here for a long time and talk about that issue, but my essential position is that as long as we have an arms race which sucks in around $1 trillion from the total amount of world capital available, we will have a shortage of capital. We are paying the price for the arms race. The total amount of U.S. savings is not enough to pay off the
Agricultural Stabilization Act
American deficit. They must maintain a strong dollar and high interest rates in order to attract capital to pay off their deficit. We have to compete and also maintain a high interest rate in order to keep some of that capital here. Given that, we begin to realize that the farmers, workers, consumers and small business people are the people who are paying for the arms race. As long as the arms race continues to suck this capital into non-productive activity, farmers are going to be in trouble, as they are in the U.S. and here in Canada; small business will be in trouble; we will have slow economic growth. The real solution has to come through stopping the insane arms race, which I am sure is destroying the Soviet economy just as it is destroying our economy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always with pleasure and interest that I to rise to take part in the debate in the House. Today, the House is considering Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities is a matter of vital importance for Canadian farmers, and especially for farmers and producers in the Maritimes. The former Liberal Government understood this when it introduced Bill C-50 last year, and now, after seven months in power, it is high time the present Government introduced a Bill that meets the expectations of the groups concerned. Unfortunately, however, Bill C-25 is not what Maritime producers and farmers expected it to be. It is disappointing because it provides no solution to the increasingly serious problems being caused by the differences in agricultural prices among the various provinces.
This Government is talking about stabilizing agricultural prices. But what kind of stabilization? Does the Bill allow for the diverse problems facing each of our ten provinces individually? Does the Bill take into consideration that production costs in the Maritimes, for instance, are higher? It does not, Mr. Speaker. We are talking about a national tripartite plan for red meat producers without even looking at the specific situation in each province.
Before further considering this policy, I would like to recall the reasons that make it necessary to have coherent legislation on farm price stabilization. This legislation provides for stabilization payments for a certain number of commodities referred to as designated commodities when prices fall below previously set levels. Similarly, most provinces have, at some time or another, introduced their own price support or income insurance programs in response to the needs of their farmers. In some provinces, the role played by the provincial threshold is essential. Since the Agricultural Stabilization Act is aimed at providing adequate support levels for all producers when necessary, and since this is a goal that is difficult to achieve, the role played and the assistance given by the provinces becomes even more crucial.
However, under this legislation, the Federal Government has paid about $200 million to red meat producers since 1978.
4930

May 21, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
For ten years, the federal and provincial governments have been working on an income stabilization program for red meat producers. Recently, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta agreed to participate, together with the federal administration and national producer organizations, in setting up a new contributory stabilization program in the red meat sector. In the Atlantic Provinces, however, producers felt that the provinces should also be able to provide financial assistance. Producer associations in the Maritimes would like to see the solution on a regional rather than provincial basis. I think their position is quite understandable. Their position is that additional funds provided to producers would help the Eastern Provinces to remain competitive on national and international markets.
Finally, in New Brunswick, as in other Maritime Provinces, there is agreement on the concept of setting up a national farm price stabilization plan. However, if the plan is to be effective and fair for all Canadian farm producers, the Government must include the provinces and give them the option of adding financial funding if necessary. This way, should there be a difference between sale prices and production costs, agricultural products will still be competitive on the markets.
In fact, that is the crux of the problem. For instance, if we compare the cost of producing one hog in Ontario and in the Maritime Provinces, we are astonished to realize that producers in the Maritime Provinces spend $6.67 more on each hog. Multiply tht figure by the impressive number of hogs in our provinces and you will see why our pork producers pay thousands of dollars more. Obviously, our production costs being higher, the product has to sell for more to be profitable. Given the difference in production costs from one province to the next, the losing province has to make up the difference by giving additional assistance. This way the provincial stabilization program restores proper balance.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure other people realize as I do that Government Bill C-25 falls short of the mark. The problems faced by the Maritime Provinces are there, they exist, they are real, and something has to be done to solve them. I know what the problems are and, for their part, the various Maritime Provinces producers associations deplore them and fully expect the federal Government to take action. For instance, here is what the Pork Producers Association of N.S. said to the Government in a recent document:
The Pork Producers Association of N.S. cannot support the proposed Tripartite Red Meat Stabilization Plan until such time as the regional differences in the cost of pork production unique to the Maritimes are recognized and alleviated. Nova Scotia producers are extremely reluctant to give up their provincial program for the Tripartite Plan.

I do not see how it could be clearer, Mr. Speaker. According to the same association, quarterly instead of weekly payments
as provided under Bill C-25 represent a losing proposition of producers.

Even with the same support or stabilization price, a weekly administered plan provides higher support than one based on average prices for the quarter.

This means that under the provincial program, the producer receives three times the amount received under the tripartite plan.
Admittedly, the difference in funding is very substantial indeed. With figures like these, it is understandable that Maritime Producers are very disturbed at the prospect of total elimination of provincial programs.
In fact, the Hog Producers Association of the Maritime Provinces insists that regional differences in production costs in the Maritimes must be acknowledged and considered when developing a stabilization program. It is absolutely essential, since the difference in production costs between Ontario and the Maritimes continues to increase very significantly.
The hog grower associations are not the only ones dissatisfied with Bill C-25. There is also the Maritime Farmers Council, an organization that represents 80 per cent of farm producers in the Maritimes and which also represents the three provincial farm federations and co-operatives in the Atlantic Provinces.
However, before discussing the demands of the Maritime Farmers Council here in the House, I would like to emphasize the importance of feed grain and the cost of grain used to feed livestock and poultry in the Maritime Provinces. First of all, feed represents about 70 per cent of the cost of raising one pig. Consequently, feed costs are the single most important factor that determines whether or not the hog growing industry will make a profit at the end of the year.
Aware of the impact equitable grain prices would have on all provinces, in August 1984, the previous Government revised the Feed Freight Assistance Program by granting $2 more per ton of grain being shipped from Western Canada to the Maritimes.
This decision by the former administration had been greatly appreciated by the agricultural producers, but there is still a lot of ground to cover because the feed grain cost difference between the Maritimes and the rest of Canada remains an unsolved issue. If the Government does not take immediate action, within a few years we stand to lose from 4,000 to 5,000 jobs in industries related to cattle breeding in the Maritimes. Otherwise, with a coherent policy, those industries might well create 4,000 to 5,000 jobs.
To be perfectly frank, the pork industry is ailing, particularly in the Maritime Provinces. In other words, it will vanish from the market before the end of next year unless preventive measures are taken as soon as possible. For example, close to
May 21, 1985

20 per cent of New Brunswick producers are practically bankrupt as it is. The first explanation for this situation, of course, is that pork prices throughout North American are depressed. The second reason is the fact that there is a wide gap in feed grain costs between the Maritimes and the rest of Canada, particularly Ontario.

On February 1, 1985, according to information provided by the Livestock Feed Board of Canada, the average cost of hog grower ration in Ontario was $207 per tonne, compared with $254 in the Maritimes, a difference of $47 per tonne. These food cost disparities between the Maritimes and central Canada are growing wider every year. Continuation of this trend will eventually threaten the survival of all sectors of our Maritime livestock industry. In the Maritime Provinces we produce 45 per cent of our annual requirement of feed grains and less than 5 per cent of our vegetable protein concentrates. The remainder is imported from central and western Canada.

So as to balance the costs of feed grains throughout the country, in 1941 the federal Government set up the Feed Freight Assistance Program under which Ottawa paid 90 per cent or more of the cost of transporting grain from Thunder Bay to the various regions of Eastern Canada. Since they did not have to worry about grain transport costs, eastern producers remained competitive on the markets. The price of feed grain was then the same for all Canadian producers. That is what the then Liberal administration wanted to achieve, as the Hon. Maurice Sauve said at the time when he was the Minister responsible.

The policy has been to pay the transportation costs of grain from Port Arthur to eastern Canada, leaving no balance of cost to the producer. This is what we have called equalization. It is an equalization or elimination of transportation costs so that the normal cost of feed would be the same as if the feed has been purchased at Port Arthur.

In 1976, federal feed freight assistance dropped from 90 per cent to 60 per cent. Even worse, in 1985 the Government is reducing feed freight assistance from 60 to 28 per cent on corn from Ontario and to 33 per cent on grain from Western Canada. This reduction is unacceptable to Maritime producers. The Government must change its feed freight assistance policy as soon as possible and allocate additional funds. Federal aid must be revised upward to 60 per cent in other words, to its 1976 level. Meanwhile, producers in the Maritimes are monitoring the situation and taking steps in the hope that by the year 2000, the provinces in Eastern Canada will be self-sufficient in feed grain. The Government will, of course, have to promote this self-sufficiency by introducing assistance and research programs. Unfortunately, all this Government is proposing to do is to cut subsidies and, most recently, to
Adjournment Motion
increase the cost of inspection services for potato, pork and beef producers.
Mr. Speaker, the Government should act quickly and effectively to help the pork industry in Eastern Canada compete with the industry in other provinces and in the United States. This kind of policy is urgently required, because the economic situation and the financial resources of farm producers make it impossible for them to make a profit. Farm producers simply cannot cover the additional cost without this threatening the existence of a number of farm operations.
Finally, if our Canadian farmers are to supply the domestic market and be competitive on international markets, we must first resolve the problems I have mentioned throughout this debate. I say yes to a farm price stabilization plan, provided it is fair to all provinces and the provinces will be able to take part in setting up the program.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to move second reading of all three Bills that you have just mentioned: Bill C-46, to amend the Divorce Act; Bill C-47 and Bill C-48, the Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act. I am pleased to have the opportunity to do so. If the House adopts the legislation that is placed before it and once the Justice Committee has dealt with it, and perhaps made some improvements or changes if it appears to be required, I believe that we will have significantly improved the social legislation of Canada in this area.
The principles of the three Bills are based on the view that in the past there has been too much emphasis placed on the grounds for divorce and too little emphasis placed on what the consequences of divorce were or are for the parties and their children. It is based on the view that the divorce laws should be part of the solution rather than part of the problem in the difficult area of family relationships and family law.
It is also based on the view that once a marriage relationship has broken down irretrievably that we should sever the legal relationship with as little stress and acrimony as possible. Those are the principles that lie behind this legislation. We should stress any possibility there might be for reconciliation or mediation.
It is a fact that marriage breakdown occurs in our society. It is an unfortunate fact of life, but it is a fact. Therefore, legislation is required to settle the issues that arise once a marriage has broken down. It is the need to update and modernize our laws in this respect that leads to the introduction of this legislation.
The Divorce and Corollary Relief Bill seeks to update the 1968 Divorce Act by modifying the grounds for divorce, by improving provisions relating to support and custody and divorce procedure. The Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act will provide additional remedies to help enforce support and custody arrangements made in the case of separation or divorce.
I might mention that legislation along these lines was introduced last year by Mr. Justice MacGuigan. The divorce part of this legislation is based in large part on that with what I believe are significant improvements, taking in mind the objections and criticisms that were made last year when that Bill was initially introduced. Among the major improvements I believe will be found the Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act to provide for the better enforcement of support and custody orders.
Let me deal first with the reform of the Divorce Act. That was a priority outlined in the Throne Speech of the Government. It is a priority because there is mounting pressure to modernize the law. The pressure comes from the public, the legal profession and various women's groups. The provincial governments, which are generally responsible for the administration of justice, have also urged us to proceed with divorce reform. These pressures are due to the conditions that have changed since the law was last reformed 17 years ago.
Last year in Canada there were approximately 69,000 divorces. There were 179,000 marriages. That is a ratio of 2.5 marriages for every divorce. Canada's rising divorce rate and the declining marriage rate have led some people to declare that the institution of marriage is in decline. Some believe that what they call shorter divorce will only contribute to a further weakening of the family. In my opinion, that is not so. If I thought that were so, I would not be introducing this Bill.
Let us look at some of the facts. Although people are divorcing in greater numbers, they are also forming new relationships. Statistics Canada estimates that three-quarters of all divorced couples remarry at one time or another. We know that of the marriages that took place in 1983, 27 per cent were composed of couples where at least one of the spouses had been previously divorced. The family is not disappearing in Canada; it is taking on new forms. People who get divorced usually wish to be remarried, to form families and carry on the family relationships.

May 21, 1985

Marriages in Canada are under the same economic and social pressures experienced by those who live in all western nations. However, statistics show that our divorce rate is modest when compared to our neighbours. The United States, Denmark and Sweden experience much higher rates of divorce. The divorce rate in Canada is similar to those in the western Commonwealth nations, such as the United Kingdom and Australia.
As members know, according to the present Act, grounds for divorce are fault oriented. The commonly used ones are adultery and cruelty. The grounds of sodomy, bestiality, sexual aggression or homosexuality are largely ignored. When a fault ground is used directly, no period of separation is required at all. For separation to be a basis for divorce, the parties had to be living separate and apart because of the conduct of the respondent at the time of the presentation of the divorce petition. The only neutral possibility in the present law is that the spouses will be separated for three years by mutual agreement before they file a petition for divorce. Otherwise, the ground is fault oriented.
A major criticism of the present system is that it focuses overly on the alleged fault of the spouse or spouses. It polarizes a conflict situation. It creates increased tension. It discourages reconciliation. The present law does all of those things. The present system denies social realities because in more than 90 per cent of all divorce actions, the issues are uncontested at the time the divorce petition is heard and the divorce is the outcome of an agreement between the spouses. That is the actuality.
In addition, an accusation of fault is certainly not conducive to mediation of the possible consequences of divorce. If we want divorce to occur in the proper kind of atmosphere and in the proper circumstances, where the parties think what is the best way of dealing with the problem, what is the best way of looking after the children for whom we are now responsible, then we need to remove the fault grounds and deal with the consequence that a particular marriage has broken down. The legislation proposes that reform should focus on the consequences of divorce rather than on the possible grounds. If we are not going to use fault direclty as a ground for divorce, then the requirement of a long separation period as evidence of marriage breakdown simply forces the parties to build separate lives and minimizes any chance of adjustment or reconciliation.
Parties who agree to divorce tend to use at the present time the fault grounds so they do not have to wait three years. Yet if they choose to complete three years of separation, one spouse still has to petition against the other. It is still an atmosphere of conflict-antagonism and fault. If one has to petition against the other, they both need separate lawyers to negotiate a settlement of the consequences. That will be done away with if this legislation is approved.
Under the present system the granting of maintenance to a spouse is often based as well on fault considerations that have
Divorce Acts
no connection with the real needs of the non-wage earning spouse. These fault considerations are used mainly to deny or decrease the right to or the amount of maintenance awarded to a dependent spouse who is found to be at fault. It is never used to increase the maintenance obligations of the wage-earning spouse who is at fault. There is an unfair application of fault considerations in this event in any case. If you are at fault but you are the wage or income producing spouse, your maintenance payment is not increased. If you are found to be at fault and are the dependent spouse, you either do not receive maintenance or your maintenance is reduced. It is not a fair situation. Mediation is not provided for.
At the present time if the divorcing spouses cannot agree upon maintenance, custody and access arrangements for the children, the issues are resolved by the court. There is no mention in the present legislation of the interests of the child. In the present legislation we are proposing, there will be only one basis or one ground for divorce, that is, marriage breakdown.
I believe the law should promote the philosophy that divorce laws are not for happy people. It is not a happy situation for those involved in a marriage breakdown. No one who is happy proceeds to a divorce. It is a remedy for an unhappy fact, that the marriage has broken down. A divorce or the grounds for it should not be a reward nor a punishment for conduct or misconduct. What is crucial is what evidence is needed to prove marriage breakdown and the most effective ways to address the consequences of the divorce.
In this legislation, we are proposing that marriage breakdown is the only basis for divorce and that it can be established in two different ways. You can prove separation for one year, or you can prove adultery or cruelty.

I will come to that in a moment.
Many people condider that if their partner has committed adultery, the marriage has broken down. The hon. gentleman might not consider that to be the case, but there are many many people, in fact the majority, I think, who happen to believe that if there is adultery or cruelty, the marriage has broken down.
The legislation we are discussing has to take account of the diverse views in this country. There are many who for religious or moral reasons believe that withholding a divorce decree where a spouse has committed adultery or cruelty is immoral. There are others who are concerned for the well being of a spouse who suffers physical or mental cruelty at the hands of the other spouse. Why should some woman, for example- usually a woman-have to stay married to her mate for a year if she is being treated with great physical cruelty or whatever? Why should she not be able to apply for divorce immediately? This Bill provides for that. There are two ways of showing marriage breakdown under this legislation. First, that you have been separated for at least a year, that the marriage has broken down despite any efforts of reconciliation. Second, if there has been physical or mental cruelty or adultery. That is a

May 21, 1985
Divorce Acts
change, by the way, from the legislation that was introduced last year.
Divorce on the basis of a fault ground provides for quicker relief from the other spouse and offers a chance to ventilate feelings, often a beneficial process. Shortening the separation period to one year from the present three years is in line with the desire to reduce the conflict between the spouses. It will also allow them to rebuild their lives more quickly. At the same time, we believe it long enough to allow for second thought and it is long enough to avoid rash and hasty divorces. If the two parties to a marriage have been living separate and apart for a year, they have not been able to patch up their differences and there is no reconciliation, the relationship has broken down and a year is certainly sufficient time to establish that. I do not think it is necessary to force people to wait another two years in addition before they can move to deal with the consequences of their marriage breakdown.
In addition, the possibility of proving marriage breakdown by fault is necessary for several reasons. First, many religious groups feel that divorce should be available immediately for moral reasons to a spouse victimized by the other. Religious beliefs and moral standards are such for certain individuals or groups that withholding a decree of divorce when it is pursued by a spouse who is the victim of adultery or cruelty would be considered immoral. For practical reasons, Mr. Speaker, we know it offers to a petitioning spouse the chance of ventilating frustrations while obtaining a judgment of divorce immediately or being granted immediate relief in the form of maintenance and or custody. That is why these grounds are being left in the legislation.
To those who favour a pure no-fault system, I answer that adultery and cruelty have long been considered valid proof of marriage breakdown and, therefore, they should stay. I can also point out that alternatives will exist and that the reduction in the separation period as an alternative means to prove marriage breakdown will render the use of fault less appealing or necessary. My guess would be that in four or five years time the use of the fault grounds will be very rare.
In addition to modifying the grounds for divorce, the principles upon which support will be provided are set out in the legislation. These do not include criteria under the present law of the conduct of the spouse. The Bill outlines the principles upon which you can obtain support. The principles do not include the conduct of the spouse. Fault is not a criteria for maintenance, nor should it be. Maintenance should be to meet the needs of a spouse, and retaining conduct as a criteria would encourage conflict between the spouses and run counter to our desire to reduce the adversarial nature of the proceedings.
In addition, this criteria has been unfairly applied in the present law. It was used to reduce maintenance received by a dependent spouse found at fault. As I mentioned before, it was never used to increase support payments owned by a supporting spouse found at fault.

speechtext:
With regard to the criteria to be applied in awarding maintenance, many groups and individuals have advocated that reference should be made specifically to the duration of and the functions performed during cohabitation in order to assess the need and quantum of maintenance. This will ensure that married people will still be free to organize as they wish the division of functions during a marriage. In the eventuality of divorce, the Divorce Act will recognize their different contributions through a maintenance order. The duration of cohabitation should be one of the criteria. If one is married for 30 years and has looked after the home for 30 years without an outside career, certainly that is a function which should influence the need for maintenance. If one has been married only two years and has been a homemaker for just two years, that would not be as significant, though it should be taken into account.
One of the problems which the Supreme Court of Canada outlined in the 1983 de cision of Messier v Delage was that the Divorce Act, that is the present Act, did not provide any guidance as to what a maintenance order was supposed to accomplish in the case of a divorce. The present Act has no objectives. It does not say whether it is to provide maintenance for life to a dependent spouse who divorces or is divorces after two or five years of cohabitation. It does not explain whether it is to provide means for a dependent spouse to become economically independent again. None of this is dealt with.
The criteria for determining what a maintenance order shold state have to be the conditions, the means and the other circumstances of the parties including the duration, the functions or the responsibilities which they performed during their cohabitation.
Our Bill proposes the following objectives for maintenance; first, that it recognize the advantages and disadvantages which arise from the marriage and the breakdown of the marriage, that it recognize the sharing of the economic burden of child care, that it recognize the relieving of economic hardship, and that where particable it lead to the achieving of economic self-sufficiency within a reasonable time. These objectives are not mutually exclusive, and they have no particular order of priority. A maintenance order should accomplish all those objectives unless one of them cannot apply.
We should note that the objective of economic self-sufficiency is a desirable one, but it is restricted in two ways. If it is not practicable, it should not apply. If it is practicable, then economic self-sufficiency should only be required to be achieved within a reasonable time. Under the present Divorce Act, the court can impose such terms, conditions or restrictions as it thinks fit and just regarding a maintenance order. For years the courts have imposed a fixed duration for maintenance in appropriate cases when economic self-sufficiency was possible. In my view, they should have that express power. It would seem to be inconsistent that such award should be
May 21, 1985

varied or revised indefinitely, but we also had to be careful of the words "fixed term".
Bill C-47 proposes certain exceptions which will alleviate injustices that such situations might create. In situations where economic hardship arises through changed circumstances related to the marriage which might have resulted in a different original order if they had existed at the time of the original order, then an application to change the conditions of the order should be received. This is an attempt to obtain a solution to a weakness which was felt to be in the legislation last year. The Bill will provide that applications can be made to change an order if the conditions change in the way that I have related. For example, there may be an incapacity on the part of an ex-spouse to become economically self-sufficient even after a fixed maintenance award term expired because of some kind of change in circumstances related to child care which could not have been contemplated at the time of the order. The Bill tries to provide for that.
With respect to children, Bill C-47 recognizes the view- and I believe it is widely accepted by all Hon. Members-that any arrangement regarding children should be according to their best interests. To give effect to this, the Bill recognizes the possibility of joint custody and that after divorce, children should have maximum access to both parents. That is the policy expressed in the Bill. The law stresses that maintenance of the children is a joint responsibility of their parents after a divorce. I think these are all steps forward.
Finally, since the present Divorce Act gives a court the power to deal with the custody of children only on the basis that the petitioner can have a divorce granted by that specific court, and since the children involved can be living somewhere else, the new legislation proposes to give a discretion to the court to transfer proceedings to the place where the children have the most substantial connection. That appears to be the most logical solution.
Under the present legislation, a divorce cannot be granted except, and I quote, "after a trial which shall be by a judge without a jury". There must be a trial under the present legislation. A costly court appearance is inappropriate in many cases, especially where both parties wish a divorce and where all the corollary issues of relief, custody and maintenance are settled. If everything is settled in a satisfactory manner, it should not be necessary to have a trial before the divorce order is granted.
Ontario has already adopted rules of procedure which will dispense with the need of a petitioner to appear in an uncontested case. The evidence then has to be in writing and supported by an affidavit. If the court is satisfied with that evidence, it can issue a decree of divorce with the appropriate maintenance or custody order. Other provinces may soon follow Ontario and, if they do, there may well be a reduction in the cost of divorce proceedings. The Bill now before the House will allow this and will give the discretion to provincial authorities.
It often happens that spouses are living in separate provinces at the time of divorce proceedings. In order to avoid the
Divorce Acts
possibility of courts in two different provinces proceeding on two actions for divorce relating to the same couple, a copy of every divorce action has to be sent to the central divorce registry here in Ottawa. This registry conducts a computer search to check to ensure that there has been no duplication of divorce proceedings. In this way, couples are ensured that the dissolution of their marriage is granted by one court with proper jurisdiction to grant the decree and to award any other relief.
As part of the Government's expenditure reduction and revenue generation initiative, a $ 10 fee will now be charged to divorcing couples for the services performed by the central divorce registry.

I think that is a fairly modest fee which people should be able to afford.
Any law which concerns itself with divorce also has to concern itself with the preservation of marriage whenever it is possible. We naturally want marriages to be preserved, and we believe in the preservation of marriages whenever possible. That is why the legislation now before the House continues the provision which was in the 1968 Act, that lawyers are required to encourage their clients to reconcile, unless that is clearly inappropriate, and they are directed to refer their clients to reconciliation services.
In addition, the Bill now before the House will replace the present provision which allowed for one 90-day period of cohabitation for the purpose of reconciliation and did not jeopardize one's status of living separate and apart. We want to take a more flexible approach, designed to encourage several attempts at reconciliation. The new Act will allow any number of attempts at living together and reconciling the total 90 days, cumulatively. In the year unfortunate couples are separated, they will be able to try to reach a reconciliation by living together again during that year for a period of up to 90 days without doing away with the fact that after the year is expired and if there is still no reconciliation they can proceed to have a divorce decree. Where a marriage is truly broken down and reconciliation has failed, we are encouraging the use of mediation to settle the questions of support for the dependent spouse, support for the children, custody and access. The use of a neutral third party trained as a mediator can often resolve those matters with less conflict and with a great deal more satisfaction than litigating them in court. The new Act will require lawyers to encourage their clients to mediate their divorces, unless that is completely inappropriate, and to refer their clients to mediation services.
We are promoting the use of mediation in ways that go beyond this Act. For example, we are providing funding for three years for a national association of mediators and others who are interested in promoting mediation. That association, known as Family Mediation Canada, is going to seek to improve communications and the exchange of ideas in that

May 21, 1985
Divorce Acts
area across Canada. It is going to seek to increase the availability of mediation services and to develop education and training standards and a code of ethics for mediators.
