This might be an area for some people I could think of to use their well honed skills.
As my time is limited, I would like to move on to the Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act. The need to improve the enforcement of support and custody orders is acute, as I am sure all Members of the House know. I have said this elsewhere, but the default rate for support payments in Canada is a national scandal. Between one-half and three-quarters of all support orders in Canada are in arrears in whole or in part. This is an intolerable situation and is the case despite the fact that research shows that a reasonable estimate is that 80 per cent of defaulting spouses can afford to make support payments. They can afford to make them, but they choose not to. That is a situation that cannot be permitted to continue. If the House passes the legislation that is now before it, that situation will continue no longer, or at least it will not continue as easily as it has heretofore.
The wholesale flouting of custody and support orders brings the authority of the courts into disrepute. It places a tremendous emotional and financial burden on the dependent spouse and on the children of the union who have to exist without the unpaid support payments. As we know, all too often most families are forced to turn to welfare, thus placing the financial burden of the defaulters on the shoulders of the taxpayers. The estimate is that $1 billion is spent annually by governments to support custodial parents and their children. One-half of that is contributed by the federal Government under the Canada Assistance Plan. Obviously any law that permits this situation to continue would be a poor law.
In some cases, a defaulting spouse is also a missing spouse. He or she cannot be located so that a support order may be enforced. Too often children are taken by the non-custodial parent in violation of a custody order and the criminal law and they disappear beyond the reach of the parent who is supposed to have custody. In such instances, the dependent spouse or custodial parent often does not have the financial resources to trace the missing spouse or child in order to enforce the support or custody order. We all know how difficult it is to enforce these orders in a country with 10 provinces, all having different court systems and different laws. We have had to develop initiatives to improve the enforcement of such orders and these initiatives have to meet the constitutional conditions that govern us in Canada.
Canada operates under a federal system. There is one federal Government, 10 provincial Governments and two Territorial Governments. Both levels of government have their respective jurisdictions. The federal Government has jurisdiction over divorce and corollary matters to divorce, but the provinces have jurisdiction over all other incidents arising out of a marriage. Both levels of Government have an interest in
improving support and custody orders. However, the provinces are primarily responsible for the enforcement of those orders. They have the constitutional responsibility for the administration of justice and over half of such orders are made pursuant to provincial family law. They are not made as a consequence of a divorce action.
We have been consulting with the Attorneys General of the provinces to improve the enforcement of family orders. They have been very co-operative. It is with this in mind that the Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act and the Divorce and Corollary Relief Act seek to improve enforcement.
First, the Divorce Act will allow support and custody orders to be registered in any court designated by a province. That will simplify enforcement. The new Act also allows the assignment of support orders to the federal or provincial Governments so that they can enforce the orders. This is a considerable improvement. The Act will allow the courts to order a spouse both to provide security for and to pay lumpsum or periodic payments. Under the new Act, the spouse can obtain a provisional variation of a support order in the province in which he or she habitually resides and have it confirmed by a court in the province in which the erring spouse resides. That will be an advance.
The companion legislation will improve the situation pursuant to both federal and provincial laws. The Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act will provide two new remedies for the enforcement of these matters in addition to what already exists under provincial law. The first remedy will allow the release of information from designated information banks of the federal Government in order to trace a missing spouse or child where there is a breach of a support or custody order or an access right or where a charge has been laid of child abduction in contravention of a custody order pursuant to Section 250.1 or 250.2 of the Criminal Code.
The second remedy will allow the garnishment or attachment of designated federal moneys due a support defaulter for payment to the dependent spouse or other creditor. That remedy is available to enforce a support order or a support provision of an agreement where the agreement can be enforced under provincial law by garnishment or attachment.
The federal information banks that will be opened up include designated banks of the Health and Welfare Department and the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. One will not be able to search any other information bank nor will one be able to search income tax files. However, those banks that can be searched provide information on 16 million adult Canadians and can be searched if the person's name or social insurance number is provided. We are looking after the right to privacy. The Act requires court authorized to apply to the federal Government for the release of the information. The information can be released only to authorities and services responsible for enforcing the orders, including the courts, provincial enforcement services and police officers. They must keep the information they receive confidential. Only information sufficient to trace the missing person will be
May 21, 1985

released. The information to be released is his or her address and the name or address of his or her employer.
The second remedy will be available for garnishment or attachment of income tax refunds, provided the provinces agree to that, interest in Canada Savings Bonds and unredeemed matured Canada Savings Bonds, the training income supplement, unemployment insurance payments, Canada Pension Plan payments, excluding children's benefits, Old Age Security payments, Guaranteed Income Supplement payments and agriculture, dairy and grain stabilization payments. Next year we will complete a review to see if there are any other federal moneys which might be added to the Act by regulation.
A court will already have found that the spouse who was ordered to pay can afford to pay. That spouse will have been given notice of these applications. The creditor spouse will have to prove the existence of the debt default and the amount of the default. The debtor spouse will have to be notified of the proceedings. All of these safeguards exist. Once the safeguards are complied with, the attachment notice can go into effect. The garnishee summons will bind Her Majesty for one year. Numerous summonses will not have to be submitted every year in order to intercept payments. The original garnishee will be good for one year.
Some have criticized this measure by saying that there should be a national enforcement service. That would be compelling in its simplicity, but it ignores the reality of the provincial constitutional authority in this field. We believe that the improvements that are to come in provincial enforcement services such as those already in place in Manitoba and Quebec, provinces which are leading the way, together with the federal legislation, will deal in a very effective manner with the problem of defaulted support payments or child abduction arising from separation or divorce.

In conclusion, I would like to say that I believe the legislation is well deserving of the support of Members of the House. I believe the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party are supportive of the legislation in general. We know that there will be a few carping criticisms, which are bound to come from some, and that there may be legitimate criticisms from others. In any event, whether carping or legitimate, we hope that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will pay adequate attention to everyone's views and report back to the House, if we pass second reading, in order that this major reform and improvement can be put into effect before the end of June with the help of all Members in the Chamber.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext: Could I ask the Member to please speak on the motion.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am asking the House to consider the advisability of establishing a toll-free telephone line which would enable citizens to report cases of government waste and misuse of funds. It is a suggestion which I received from a constituent a number of months ago.
I did some research on this question as it applied to the United States. They have a hot line program which has been operating for about five years. It is used to ferret out the misuse of Government funds.
All citizens of our country are vitally interested in how their dolars are used or misused. Through use of this hot line an individual, whether he works in a government department, out in the field, or even a concerned taxpayer, could pick up the phone and say that such a problem exists. They might say that such and such a problem should be looked into because they think there is an abuse.
May 21, 1985

How do these abuses come about? This House authorizes the spending of millions upon millions of dollars in grants for projects to various groups or individuals in order to create jobs. There may or may not be some abuses, but if there is, a concerned citizen or civil servant could alert the Auditor General's department of that fact through this line and save the Canadian taxpayers a great deal of money.
In the U.S. a request was made for a summary of what had happened through this program after it had been operating for five years. The program had not been formally advertised, but it got a good deal of news coverage. Over a period of five years, the hot line had recorded 53,000 calls, of which 10,600 were referred to the Comptroller General. Of those 10,600, about 1,100 were substantiated; there was enough evidence to proceed to investigate and recover funds that had been misused. In fact, they were able to identify situations where $20 million to $30 million had been misspent. They projected savings of another $24 million through tightening up on improper practices.
I cite that example because I think there is a good possibility that a proportionate saving could be made in Canada. We all hear stories about the misuse of government funds. I am sure that each one of us in this House can recount stories of constituents coming forward and making certain allegations. Because of the workload we have as Members of Parliament, while we may be able to alert a department about an allegation, we are not able to carry through with an investigation on our own. That is why I am asking that a program like this be set up in Canada.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a small department of the office of the Auditor General could set up this hot line across Canada in order to receive information from the taxpayers who do not ordinarily have access to the right kind of people to lodge their complaints, and from civil servants who are afraid to say anything because they might lose their jobs. Given the experience in the United States and the amount of taxpayers' dollars which have been saved, this could well be a worthwhile program here.
If we were to establish this hot line, it would also make the taxpayers much more interested in how their tax dollar is spent. The way it is now, the taxpayer feels he has no opportunity to speak up or change in any way what is happening. All they see is big government spending big dollars. They might shake their heads about it, but the vital interest is not there because they feel they cannot do anything about it. This line would give them a chance to do something about it. As well, I think it would clearly indicated to civil servants that they are charged with a special responsibility to jealously guard taxpayers' dollars. Therefore, I think if this is done, over a period of years we would see a much more responsible attitude on the part of the Public Service toward the public purse. We would also see a much greater concern expressed by individual taxpayers over how their tax dollars are being spent.
I know that others might wish to comment on my suggestion, so I will close by giving the House some indication of the types of calls which have been received by this hot line in the
Misuse of Funds
U.S. See if this is not familiar to us all. One caller alleged that space rented by the General Services Administration in a New York City office building had been vacant for months. That certainly reminds me of some of the accusations that were made in this House by Members on this side when we were in opposition, and indeed by members of the Opposition today. There is space being rented by government agencies and departments right across this country which has remained vacant for months or years. Yet we here do not know how these allegations are being investigated. As another example, an anonymous informant claimed that two university professors in Wisconsin had extorted money from trainees in a federal program and converted federal funds to their personal use. I know that there are federal funds being used in training programs across the country. There is potential for the same type of abuse as in this example.
An anonymous caller said an employee of the Department of the Interior in the State of Virginia was using a Government account with a local auto dealer to embezzle money. These things would never come to light unless taxpayers who see an abuse of trust or of the spending of tax dollars have the ability to pick up the phone and report such abuses. Another informant sent a photograph of a veteran, who was on full disability, operating a commercial fishing boat in Texas. That informant, who was a taxpayer, did not agree that the veteran should be ripping off the system. An informant alleged that a Major General, the commanding officer of an army installation, bought an interest in a nearby hotel after being advised by the Department of Defence of a planned troup increase and possible housing shortage at the installation.
I am sure that other Members could think of examples of misuse of Government funds. Such a system would give taxpayers the opportunity to more actively participate in the correction of abuses. Public civil servants and Crown corporation employees would become much more attuned to the concept that they are indeed spending taxpayers' money and that they are accountable for it. I hope that Hon. Members will take a positive attitude toward this suggestion. The results could be well worthwhile and show a considerable saving to the entire country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Member for giving me this golden opportunity to speak of Government waste. There could be no more valuable occasion, outside of Question Period, to raise such issues. I am very pleased that we have this motion before us today. I shall have to introduce such a motion myself in order to bring up all the incidents of Government waste in the country.
One of the first issues of Government waste that I would like to deal with is the fact that the House wasted eight minutes waiting for the Hon. Member. Members are paid roughly $30 an hour. You have told us in the past, Mr. Speaker, that all Members are always present in the House. Therefore, we can only assume that every other Member was

May 21, 1985
Misuse of Funds
here. Therefore, multiplying $4 by 281 other Members, we see that it cost the taxpayers of the country $1,124 for the eight minutes that we waited for the Hon. Member to show up here today. Two weeks ago the Member did not show up at all. We wasted one hour which cost $7,858. Add that to the $1,124 wasted today, and we have a grant total of $8,992 of wastage caused by the Hon. Member for failing to show up to debate his own issue in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member across the way said that we should raise other examples of Government waste in the House. As much as I hate to, I am about to do so. Let us start at the top, Mr. Speaker. The Leader himself increased the budget of his own office by 57 per cent this year after telling everyone else in the country that it was time to tighten the belt. We can see that there is an awful lot of slack in the belt of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
The Government handed out a number of jobs, some 1,200 of which are listed here in this black paper. They were mostly given to Tory friends and relatives. Two of those jobs are particularly notorious. One was given to an individual by the name of Lawrence Hanigan, the defeated Tory candidate in the riding of Laval-des-Rapides. The other one was given to Mr. Roy McMurtry, the former Attorney General of Ontario. Both of these individuals were appointed to high paying Tory rewards. That is enough to make some Conservative backbenchers in the House wish that they had lost so that they too could have partaken in such rewards. However, unfortunately for them and for us, the Tory back-benchers were elected and could not receive the high paying rewards of $100,000 each.
Well, the $100,000 salaries were not enough for Mr. Hanigan and Mr. McMurtry. The Government decided to help them make ends meet in their budgets. The Government gave them pay increases of $38,000 each to ensure they had enough money to pay the grocery bill at the end of the month, which likely comes free with that kind of job to start with.
We have since nicknamed Thursday, November 8, "Black Thursday." On that day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) perpetrated his vicious attack on the people of Canada. He decided that he would cut just about everything for the poor people of the country. The Minister of Finance decided to send copies of this notorious statement to his colleagues, the Tory Premiers of the country. It cost $23,850 in jet service to deliver a speech that should not have been read to start with. That would have cost $105 by Air Express. The sense of economics of the Government led it to believe that the proper thing to do was to waste $23,850 in order to do a $105 job. That is an example of Government waste.
Let us talk about the Shamrock summit in Quebec City. It cost us $525,000 to hear about the Irish eyes that were smilling. Notwithstanding that the singing was not much to start with, the price of the affair was enough to give indigestion to everyone who ate the caviar and quail that was served. The total cost of the event was $1 million to the taxpayers of the country.
The summit was supposed to be for good Canada-U.S. relations. Well, no sooner had the President of the United States flown home than there were countervail duties on Canadian pork and other products. That was the effectiveness of that endeavour. It was another waste of taxpayers' dollars.
Around Christmas time the Prime Minister decided that he should take a little holiday to Florida. Maybe he was right and he should have taken that holiday to Florida.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext: With a one-way ticket.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext:
My friend says that perhaps he should have taken a one-way ticket. While he was there, he wanted to see what the Opposition was up to. Every day he had video clips flown to Florida. The cost of flying the video clips to Florida to enable the Prime Minister to watch the Opposition on television was $1,000.
Let us talk about another Member of the House. Perhaps-

-we might mention the "national air draft", Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) who was described in those terms when he was a Minister in Quebec. He took it upon himself to take off for various destinations at the expense of Canadian taxpayers. The Minister chose to fill a jet with relatives, department officials and what have you and fly to the Middle East for a ribbon-cutting ceremony for which Canadian taxpayers had to shell out $57,000, Mr. Speaker.
Those are examples of waste of funds by this Government. [English]
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) decided to take a trip to Vancouver on board a government jet. She arrived there three minutes ahead of Air Canada. The cost was $17,000. It cost us $5,000 a minute to send the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to Vancouver. That is a prime example of Government waste.
Let us talk about renovations to the offices of Cabinet Ministers. They are the ones who tell the people of Canada that it is time to tighten the belt. Let us hear about Government waste. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) decided that it would require $10,000 to renovate his office on Parliament Hill. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) required $22,327. That will buy a lot of wallpaper and paint.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), the cutting man himself who is the watchdog of our tax dollars, requires $7,887. The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek), or the amateur Minister of Fitness and Sport, as he is sometimes called, required $13,496. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) required $7,950. The Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton), whoever that is, required $17,712 to redo the inside of the Parliament Hill office.
May 21, 1985

As if that is not enough, add $173,000 worth of new limousines which make the West Door of the House of Commons look like a used car lot. They are added to the ones that were already there. Of course, one cannot have limousines without chauffeurs. One cannot have chauffeurs without political commissaires and chiefs of staff, which every Cabinet Minister has. They are paid the mere sum of $80,000 each, courtesy of the taxpayers of our country.
What about car rentals? It is not enough to have that used car lot outside the West Door, in the first three months of this year the Government had to rent another $30,000 worth of cars to make up for the shortage of cars to drive Cabinet Ministers around.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is Government waste. How about the $36 million of Government waste in order to colour our military differently because the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen), who has lost his coat over this issue, cannot differentiate one person in the military from another? It seems that everyone else could, but he could not.
Let's talk about chiefs of staff, about staff for the Prime Minister. Let's talk about nannies and about Ministers who spend $496,000 in their first few months in office on jet travel alone. My colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), reminds me that not all was wasted. The Prime Minister himself paid $1.50 for every meal that he ate at his house. He reimbursed the people of Canada. Let me remind the House that most citizens of this country would gladly change their grocery bill for $1.50 per head per meal. I wish I could, frankly, and I am sure that most of my constituents could not feed their family on $1.50 a meal.
Last week we heard that the Government spent $103,000 in advertising a program which was signed in 1981 and took effect a year ago. The Government believes that now is the time the program should be advertised. What did it do? It gave a contract to the R. T. Kelley Advertising Agency, which is run by a former Ontario Conservative Cabinet Minister and former defeated Tory candidate in the riding of Hamilton West. They gave this $103,000 contract.

Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) being embarrassed by these examples of Government waste. Were I Tory right now-heaven forbid-I am sure that I would be as embarrassed as the Hon. Member.

It would cost us $50,000 a year so that that Member and other Conservative backbenchers could do their jobs.
I have an easier solution. I invite all people to contact me at area code 613-996-2907. They can report all Government wastes at 996-2907.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to sit in the House and hear the comments by the Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) who introduced this motion and to the comments by the Liberal spokesperson, the Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). It is interesting to hear the Liberals and Tories debating about who is the most gross when it comes to getting into the trough.
I listened with some interest to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell talk about renovations, nannies and advertising. We must mention the extensive renovations carried out by the former Liberal Prime Minister. We must keep in mind the extensive renovations to Stornoway that are now being considered. We are intrigued when we hear about nannies. We recognize that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) needed a nanny. We certainly understood that the previous Prime Minister needed a nanny.
We heard talk about advertising. I remember well, during the Constitution debate, the Liberal geese flying across our television screens. In fact, I think most Canadian people felt, after seeing these geese, that they were being goosed. I believe that that perception by Canadians was quite accurate.
The Hon. Member for Athabasca is proposing this resolution in the midst of the flowering of Tory patronage. He does so without a blush, just as the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell reads his list without blushing. I believe that the Liberals, with their long experience, have become experts at going to the trough. Perhaps the only difference between the Liberals and the Tories, who have been away from the trough for such a long time, is that the Liberals had developed some table manners. At least they wore a bib when they were at the trough. The Tories have been away so long that they are madly rushing to the trough to distribute what they can. I

May 21, 1985
Misuse of Funds
suggest that Canadians are upset at the method of Conservative patronage.
I think Canadians have become a bit cynical about political parties generally. I wonder what they must feel about the Prime Minister who, during the election campaign, wrapped himself in such righteous indignation. He condemned in ringing and eloquent terms the patronage in which the Liberals indulged just before the former Prime Minister left and the ascendency of the new Liberal leader. When the former Opposition Leader became Prime Minister, gone was the cloak of self-righteousness. He and his fellow Tories jumped into the trough. It is hoped over these next four years at least that some table manners are developed by the Government.
I think Canadians are concerned about the type of waste that does occur on a patronage level, but this is nickel and dime stuff really and is something Canadians generally expect. I certainly expect a certain amount by any political party that forms a Government. I think it is a question of degree. As well, it is a question of ability. If you are a Conservative government and appoint a Conservative person to a board, I will stand in my place right now and say there is nothing particularly wrong with that. The sin is if that person is not capable of carrying on the proper function to which he was appointed. It is on that level we must question some of the appointments which the present Government has made. We must also question some of the appointments which the previous Government made. Mr. Mackasey, for example, was appointed to Air Canada and other various spots. Surely some secret moments were enough to make even Mr. Mackasey blush. It is not political affiliation but the lack of ability in carrying out the function which is the biggest sin.
When we are talking about Government waste, the big item, it appears we have lost over $2.5 billion to $2.8 billion on an R and D tax credit scheme. Originally when this measure was introduced by the Liberal Minister of Finance, it was to cost the treasury $500 million in lost revenue. Everyone agrees it has become a scam. It is as though the doors of the treasury were flung wide open and we lost $2.8 billion. This is a big money item, Mr. Speaker. Nobody in this House will claim that we have had $2.8 billion in extra research and development here. If we had $2.8 billion more in research and development, we would be in quite a different situation today. It is apparent to all of us that the only research and development which this tax measure has created is research and development by accountants and tax lawyers.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext: All Tories.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext:
Here we have a big budget item, $2.8 billion, which is $2.3 billion more than was estimated. It is "Oops", a $2.3 billion "oops". Then we have Mirabel Airport. Another billion dollar "oops". This was thought out by some bureaucrats in the Department of Transport who really like thinking in tremendous Technicolor screens, the same people who are destroying agriculture in western Canada by the Crow Bill
which the Liberal Government was so stupid to push through and which the Tories have not revoked. These same people are the ones who projected the need for this tremendously large airport outside of Montreal which is a disaster. Everybody admits now that it is a billion dollar "oops" in lost change that fell out of a pocket.
The money on these two programs, the R and D tax credit and Mirabel, would do a lot to alleviate the hardships in which unemployed people are finding themselves. It amazes me that Governments, whether Liberal or Tory, are quite willing to nickel and dime people who are poor, sick, or elderly. They are quite willing to restrict the eligibility for unemployment insurance so they can squeeze $200 million out of the scheme.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext: The tough Tories.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT WASTE ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLL-FREE TELEPHONE LINE
speechtext:
Yet do we find the same concern when we lose $2.3 billion in this R and D tax scheme? No, Mr. Speaker. There is hardly a word about it. We do not talk about these welfare bums, or the lazy people who, if you only give them an extra squeeze, would get off their fannies and find a job. There is none of this rhetoric. It seems that we are quite willing to lose $2.3 billion in this mad hatter R and D tax scheme. There is not a ripple of protest. Yet we have all the wrath, fury, and self-righteousness directed at the poor soul who is on unemployment insurance. There might be some odd cheat in the unemployment world. Human beings are human beings, but the rip-offs that occur in unemployment insurance are nothing compared to the rip-off now occurring with the R and D tax credit scheme. All the focus is on the poor soul who is trying to get by on a few hundred bucks a week.
When the Hon. Member suggests that we set up a hot line so people can report on Government wastage, are they going to report on the guy next door who someone might figure should not be eligible for his welfare or his unemployment insurance cheques? After all, it is Government wastage. Will this be something like a crime watch, except it is on the civil service? Is this part of the extension of the civil service bashing in which Members opposite seem to indulge? Who are they going to phone? What are they going to phone about? Are they going to phone about government wastage in terms of advertising? What about the Liberal flying geese?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not a bit upset by the remark of the Hon. Member. Certainly he is not a pearl, and everyone recognizes that his fanciful Bill is not one either. If it was, he would have made certain that he was here at the beginning of the debate. It was supposed to be dealt with a week or so ago and he did not bother showing up, and he showed up late today. Obviously it is not a pearl with which we are dealing. I recognize the general level of intellect of the Hon. Member in politics and so forth. What he said to me was of no great surprise. I do not feel insulted. That type of insult by that type of Hon. Member reflects rather well on me and identifies the Hon. Member and what he is all about.
Let me return to the Bill which is before us. It is sort of a crime stopper Bill on public servants which the Hon. Member is requesting Parliament to consider. The first question I would ask is: On what are they reporting? Can they pick up the telephone and say that there is government wastage as a result of the proposed renovations to the summer residence of the Prime Minister or to the residence of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), or that they think there is wastage as a result of the R and D tax credit? On what will they report? My second question is: To whom will they report?
If we have a system which works properly, and if we have a Government which recognizes the important role that Members of Parliament can and should be playing, it is the role or job of Members of Parliament to get those telephone calls. They should hear from their constituents and from the
Misuse of Funds
Canadian public that they believe there is government waste on some project or other.
Public waste is an important topic. All Governments should be concerned about curbing waste and about running a tight and well administered operation. However, to do what the Hon. Member is asking will not accomplish that purpose. In fact, the result will be that public servants will be afraid. They will have the sense that they are being spied on all the time and that they have to account for policies and programs for which they are very often not responsible. Very often public servants are just people who are carrying out the duties and directions of their political masters. If things do not go right, they are the men and women who get blamed. They are the people who are held up to ridicule. They are the victims of public servant bashing. Very often the political masters who are really to blame escape it.
Possibly this becomes more odious under Tory Governments, in that the Tories really enjoy public servant and bureaucrat bashing. Very often when they form the Government, it is the directions which they give to the public servants that create the mistakes for which the public servants are blamed. Back home in Saskatchewan we see this time and again. Even though there is a Conservative Government in the Province of Saskatchewan, they continue to bash public servants; they continue to bash their own employees and blame them for their own mistakes. That is the most deplorable part of all.
I should like to turn to the role of the Auditor General, who is really the watch-dog on government waste. I believe the Auditor General should have a firm mandate. He should have access to all pertinent documents in order to make a decision as to whether or not there is gross government waste. When the Conservatives were in Opposition, they were all in favour of that concept. Unfortunately, now that they are in Government, with perhaps documents they would rather not have the Auditor General see, they do not want to give that power to him any longer. Perhaps they want a free telephone line to Ottawa with some bureaucrat at the other end taking all the complaints. Then perhaps they can feel they have done their job in terms of accountability for public expenditures. The Auditor General has the capacity, the mandate, the technical know-how and staff to do the job properly. If it is serious about government waste, one of the first things it should do is strengthen the role of the Auditor General.
Another question I would have if the service is set up is: How would the complaints and comments be responded to? Will someone take a complaint and pass it on to another person, to be passed on to a third person, so that it is eventually lost in a labyrinth of memos and cross-memos? Again I return to the role of Members of Parliament. We should receive those telephone calls. The Canadian public or our constituents should fee, regardless of whether their Member of Parliament is a Conservative, a Liberal or a New Democrat, regardless of whether he or she is a member of the Government or of the Opposition, free to pick up the telephone to tell us that they think there is a case of abuse or a case of

May 21, 1985
Adjournment Debate
gross wastage. I am not referring to petty stuff, but to gross wastage. Then we should have the ability as Members of Parliament to follow through on the complaints. We should be able to talk to Ministers and to Deputy Ministers to obtain an understanding of what is going on and to get to the bottom of whether or not it is a legitimate complaint. This means a strengthening of the role of ordinary Members of Parliament. As well it means a strengthening of our role in committee and a touch less bipartisan politics. When government or opposition Members come across instances of government waste, they should not be out there to score political points. They should help to make Government more effective and work better for the public of Canada. We should all be able to co-operate in that effort. If we receive suggestions from our constituents on how to make Government more effective, we should have the ability and capacity to see that those suggestions are followed through and implemented. However, it means a different concept of what this place is all about and what we as Members of Parliament are all about. It means a different concept of how Government, Parliament and the committees work. Lacking that, I am afraid the Private Member's Bill which is before us is quite inadequate. I tend to think it is a Mickey Mouse public relations gesture. I see that it is six o'clock. I assume the Bill dies.

subtopic: TRADE-BEEF IMPORT QUOTAS. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S ROLE
TRADE-BEEF IMPORT QUOTAS. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 14, I put a question to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) concerning the press reports indicating that the Government had agreed to increase the quotas of European Economic Community beef coming into Canada from 5.9 million pounds to some 23.5 million pounds. On December 21, the Government triggered the meat import law and imposed a quota on European meat of 5.9 million pounds. This quota was well in tune with the amount of meat which had been coming into Canada in the previous four or five years. It was a sharp reduction for the EEC, but was certainly well within historic averages.
Some time late in January or February, we heard that the Government was considering caving in to pressure being put on
it by the EEC. I do not know why it would do so. Clearly the beef which came to Canada last year was meat that was surplus within the European Economic Community. It was highly subsidized to cover the cost of transportation into Canada. In spite of this, we heard reports that the Government was going to cave in and abandon the red meat producers of this country by increasing those quotas.
I put the question to the Minister for International Trade. In his response, he indicated that the Government had initially an agreement with, I assume, the negotiators. However, he could not reveal the amount of the agreement. I think the Minister has a responsibility to come clean with the House of Commons and the industry which has suffered so much in the past six months by revealing exactly what is taking place.
Many of the agricultural producers of the country feel that they have been let down by the Government. The Government did trigger the meat import law. However, it took the Government three months to make up its mind, even though strong representations were made all fall for it to trigger the meat import law. In spite of that, no action was taken for this calendar year until December 21.
We must put this matter in perspective. The Government has already raised the United States quota from some 21 million pounds to some 65 million pounds of meat. There are rumours that a secret agreement has been reached to increase the Nicaraguan quota from some 600,000 pounds to over 9 million pounds and that even that estimate may be low due to the trade embargo placed by the United States on Nicaragua.
Naturally, agricultural groups, farm groups, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are just appalled at the prospect of the federal Government backing down and knuckling under by agreeing to an increase of some 17 million pounds of additional beef coming into the country. This amount of beef would represent at least 1,000 carcasses of meat which is subsidized by 40 cents to 48 cents a pound.
I would like to read into the record excerpts of a letter from the Bruce County Federation of Agriculture dated April 30, 1985. This letter was addresed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and a copy was sent to me as Liberal agriculture critic. The letter reads:
We, as members of the Bruce County Federation of Agriculture, live in the foremost beef producing County in Ontario. To say the least, we are more than concerned about increasing the allotment of EEC beef into this country.
We find it very difficult to understand at a time when the red meat industry in this country is in an unfathomable financial crisis, with a record high number of bankruptcies, why a supposedly concerned and caring government would allow even one single pound more of beef into this country.
At a time of decreasing beef consumption and low commodity prices that don't even come close to covering the cost of production, it would hardly seem like a prudent financial move.
With all of this in mind, we respectfully request an explanation from your office outlining the reasons for such a decision being made when we all know the result would be another disastrous blow to our Canadian beef industry. Doesn't our government care?
We look forward to a reply-
May 21, 1985

Well, I am not sure whether Wayne Robertson, the President of the Bruce County Federation of Agriculture, has received a reply, but, clearly, Members of the House of Commons have not received a reply from the Government on the question.
During the same Question Period, I asked the Minister for International trade if, during the recent visit of the Prime Minister to the European Economic Community countries, he had raised the question of the massive increases in beef quotas with the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Chancellor of West Germany and the President of France. I think, because the matter is of such importance to our agricultural community, that the Prime Minister should use the prestige and power of his office, either as a group or on a bilateral basis, to raise matters which are of fundamental importance to producer groups. The response which I received from the Minister for International Trade was very high-handed. He said that the Prime Minister was not there to negotiate beef agreements. Of course he was not. But, when he was meeting with senior heads of government of the European Economic Community, he should have seized the opportunity. It is a very important issue to the red meat industry in Canada. There is no reason why he could not have raised the question with the heads of government. I think the Canadian farmers and beef producers of Canada are appalled by that type of attitude.
There is more to be concerned about in this matter. Press reports have told us that Australia, which has been a traditional trading partner with Canada in red meat, and which has large access to our markets, is very concerned about the subsidized beef which is coming into Canada. The Australians feel that it will drop the price of their exports to Canada. The Australians have a very important stake in their beef exports to Canada. They are upset. In fact, I am told that Australia had offered-if the Canadian Government had summoned up the courage and gone to GATT to fight the issue rather than being a pussy-cat and backing down to the EEC-to assist Canada and fight the issue at the GATT tribunal. It is a matter of great concern. I hope the Government will not sell out the beef producers of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stewart Mclnnes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: TRADE-BEEF IMPORT QUOTAS. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with the Hon. Member that the matter of beef imports from EEC countries is one of great concern to Canadians. It is because of that that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) has been giving a great deal of attention to that issue. He has also been giving attention to a corresponding issue; that of the threat which has been made by the EEC to impose substantial quotas or tariffs on other sectors of our agricultural community-that group which intends to export to the EEC community. Both sides of the question must be taken into consideration, and that has been done.
I am happy to report that a tentative agreement has been reached with negotiators representing the European Economic Community and that the agreement has been secured. Only outstanding at this time is the ratification and formal approval
Adjournment Debate
by the Council of EEC Ministers. It is anticipated that that will come within a reasonable length of time.
It is necessary for the Minister to be sensitive to and have regard for the interests of the beef industry, which has suffered unduly because of the subsidized beef imports from the EEC. We are very much supportive of their position, and indeed the Minister has said so in the House on a number of occasions, especially on April 29 and May 14. However, the prolonged negotiations have now concluded and we hope to be able to make a more formal as well as full and final report in the very near future.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-MARITIME COMMAND-RESTORATION OF NAVY BLUE UNIFORMS
NATIONAL DEFENCE-MARITIME COMMAND-RESTORATION OF NAVY BLUE UNIFORMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in November, 1984, I received confirmation in the House of Commons from the then Minister of National Defence that the Government intended to take action to restore navy blue uniforms to Canada's Navy, and to accomplish this change in time for the celebration of the Canadian Navy's seventy-fifth anniversary, the major events of which will occur toward the end of June or early in July. I hope the Minister's representative, in commenting on this matter, will bring us up to date on the Government's and the Minister's plan for implementing the change to navy blue uniforms in Maritime Command, and also other changes in uniform which are contemplated by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen). But I come here with what I believe will be a more important message. Let me begin by reviewing very briefly my involvement in the campaign to have navy blue uniforms restored to Canada's Navy.
Early in 1983 I became aware of the desire on the part of many members of Maritime Command, Canada's Navy, to again wear a navy blue uniform. I brought the matter to the attention of the House of Commons early in 1983. Then in July of 1983 Vice Admiral James Fulton, when he turned over command of Maritime Command, indicated in that ceremony that he, as a member of Canada's Navy, desired a restoration of navy blue. In a ceremony which was attended by literally thousands of people at CFB Halifax, he said that he would like all people present there to know that those in the Navy would like to be dressed in blue and look like sailors.
I review that situation by way of saying that quite often a Member of Parliament who hears a message from a constituent, and from an important constituent such as Vice Admiral Fulton, representing as he did the personnel of Maritime Command, is prepared to take action. I think we who were

May 21, 1985
Adjournment Debate
interested were effective in bringing before the House of Commons that desire for change. Let me say very quickly, because I heard the remarks today in the House of Commons by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who deplored the Government's action in bringing about a change of uniform for Canada's Armed Forces, even though that appears to be the overwhelming desire of the personnel in Canada's Navy, that we, and I hope I speak for all Members of the Progressive Conservative Party, want to react to the desires and needs of the personnel of Canada's forces.
We cannot deliver all that they might desire in the way of equipment and facilities, but we can at least recognize those needs that we can fulfil. It was in response to that kind of request from those personnel that I think our Government acted to restore the navy blue uniform to Maritime Command and to consider other uniform changes.
This is relevant today in the House of Commons because the same person, now retired from the Canadian Armed Forces, Vice-Admiral Fulton, has made the suggestion that the Navy must make its voice heard in Ottawa. I want to tell him and all people interested in the Canadian Armed Forces that that is exactly the case. The Canadian Forces in all three commands must make their needs known to parliamentarians and public officials. They must get the message to us so that we, in turn, can get the message to the public that the Canadian Armed Forces has to be a developing institution. It cannot stand stagnant and let the world go by.
We must all take Admiral Fulton's message to heart, particularly those of us in the Progressive Conservative Party who want to support the Canadian Armed Forces. I draw a distinction between our own position and the position of the socialists in the New Democratic Party who would have us withdraw from organizations such as NATO. They would have us cut back on National Defence expenditures and destroy the spirit and capacity of our Armed Forces as though it were not part and parcel of the Canadian fabric, the Canadian nation, and the national way of life.
Admiral Fulton must convince his own colleagues in the Armed Forces, and those who have retired from the Armed Forces, that there is a need for public education. The Leader of the New Democratic Party compares National Defence expenditures to other kinds of social programs and claims that National Defence expenditures adversely affect social programs. We cannot allow such an erroneous message to go to the public. We must fight for attention for the Canadian Armed Forces. The role of those involved in the Canadian Armed Forces in this exercise is of vital importance.
I want to say to Admiral Fulton, through the medium of the House of Commons, that his message is heard. It is recognized that in the national interest we must bring to the attention of all Canadians the need for improvement in our Canadian Forces. It is part of our sovereignty and way of life. It has been since the beginning of Canada. With our conscious attention to
the needs of the Canadian Armed Forces, it will continue to be part of our national life.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-MARITIME COMMAND-RESTORATION OF NAVY BLUE UNIFORMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to respond to the Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) on behalf of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen). I am able to stand and give this response today in good part because of the efforts over many years of the Member for Halifax West. So often in the House of Commons we start with an idea, bring it forward, and then have to wait and wait for its fruition. The Member's patience and hard work has been rewarded.
I can understand that he has exerted pressure for a distinctive blue uniform for the Maritime Command. He can realize that this is only one small part of the Government's decision to provide new, distinctive uniforms for all three elements. I am sure the Maritime Command on the East Coast is pleased, as it is on the West Coast. As east meets west across the country, we will find a whole new sense of pride and increased morale in our Armed Forces.
It would be remiss of me not to mention specifically the Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates). This Member came to power in Canada with a very firm decision and a strong sense of connection with the Navy from his own home area. He recognized that morale is all important in the initial stages of the rebuilding in'which the Government is currently involved. I want to pay credit to the former Minister of National Defence today.
Keeping in mind the seventy-fifth anniversary of Maritime Command, for which the main celebrations will begin in late June and early July of this year, I am pleased to inform the Member that new uniforms will be available in appropriate numbers when the first public tatoo is presented on June 27. Indeed, we hope that the same situation will prevail for all three services. This is what we are aiming for. Accordingly, 50 per cent of the change-over will be completed by the fall of 1986. Specifically, by July 1 this summer, Naval will be in 750 winter uniforms and 500 summer uniforms. Land will have 750 winter uniforms and 400 summer uniforms. Air will have 750 winter uniforms and 400 summer uniforms.
That very tight target is in fact being met and Canadians will have their first view this summer. I am sure the Member for Halifax West will be standing at that tatoo with a very special sense of pride as he will know that his efforts have resulted in the Armed Forces marching in different uniforms.
In closing, let me stress that this is just the beginning. It is a symbol of better things to come. We have had North Warning, low level defence, new frigates and a communications system. A major policy review is under way with respect to manpower and the regulars and reserves. In spite of the economic conditions, we are maintaining our commitment to the Armed Forces, and this move is symbolic of that particular concern.
May 21, 1985

subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-COMPENSATION INQUIRY. (B) GOVERNMENT ACTION. (C) DEADLINE INQUIRY
VISIBLE MINORITIES-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-COMPENSATION INQUIRY. (B) GOVERNMENT ACTION. (C) DEADLINE INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, almost four months have passed since I raised questions in the House regarding the Government's plans to redress the injustice done to Japanese Canadians during the Second World War. At the time there was a real sense of anxiety about the possibility that the Government might act unilaterally to impose what it saw as a settlement on the Japanese Canadian community, not matter what they thought. Expectations of negotiation were raised while at the same time deadlines were suddenly imposed and unilateral action threatened. I raised questions about that and the need to achieve an agreement, as well as the possibility of early deadlines being used to cut negotiations short.
The months that have passed since then give us reason to bring this issue into focus for the nation and reveal the extent to which the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) has failed the Government, his leader and the Canadian nation. It has been a little over eight months since the Minister took office. In the first weeks of May, we heard some strange remarks from the Minister. On the one hand, in a radio interview on May 5, he declared that when he took office and found the slogan, "Celebrate our Differences" being used in his directorate, he scrapped that right off.
Inevitably, when he convened the Multicultural Conference in Winnipeg on May 14, that kind of suggestion forced him to deny that he was in fact thinking of Canada in melting pot terms. He said, "This country is never going to be a melting pot. I don't think Canadians want Canada to be a melting pot".
When he held a press conference to wrap up proceedings after this conference, he suggested that the fight against racism falls outside the jurisdiction of his Department. He said that although his Department is concerned about racism, it "really falls outside our jurisdiction". His concern would be to sensitize Canadians against racial intolerance.
Inevitably, that kind of statement led to questions in the House. Just this past Thursday, in response to questions in the House, the Minister stated:
-I and the multicultural Department have a major responsibility for the area of race relations in Canada. If you take the very narrow definition, in terms of legislation it falls in our area. We have a major thrust in terms of fighting racism at every level of society.
This evidence of indecisiveness and lack of clear leadership is nowhere more clear than in the matter of the Japanese Canadians. I call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to very carefully consider the current situation. If the need for leadership is not obvious, surely the Prime Minister's pledge to address this issue makes its attention urgent.
What we have seen over the past month, after expectations of negotiation had been clearly raised, was a press release under the heading of the multiculturalism directorate. It clear-
Adjournment Debate
ly referred to a negotiation process, the process of negotiation. What we found in January was a refusal on the part of the Minister and his officials to negotiate with the Japanese Canadians. We saw the attempt to impose deadlines to arrive at an apology and a redress formula. We saw a resolution for apology being presented to House Leaders that was not the final resolution that had been discussed in these non-negotiations. We saw a refusal on the part of the Minister to consider compensation, either individually or corporately for the Japanese Canadians. We saw a rejection of any action on the War Measures Act, on criminal charges and other concerns which the Japanese Canadians have had in years past. A variety of those items were not considered.
The Japanese Canadian community, which has been clarifying its own mind on these matters, has in the last week felt driven to undertake a consideration of the costs of the losses suffered during the 1940s. This is being done by the firm of Price Waterhouse. The process presumably will be at the expense of Japanese Canadians themselves in order to clarify their needs. The Toronto Star pointed out in the last days that the Prime Minister said last year that Japanese Canadians need assurance that:
-this kind of heinous action will never again take place in Canada and, if it does, that we will have the nerve and the courage to stand up and apologize for it and deal with it honourably.
The Prime Minister recognized they, the Japanese Canadians, were not looking for overwhelming compensation, but symbolism and reassurance. He said:
-I feel very strongly that Canadian citizens whose rights were abused and violated and trampled upon indeed should be compensated.
That very clear statement has not been acted upon by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and the honour of the nation which has been demanding redress action for months and months continues to wait. How long is this charade to go on?

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-COMPENSATION INQUIRY. (B) GOVERNMENT ACTION. (C) DEADLINE INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government views this matter as a moral issue, not an economic issue. This has been stated in a letter addressed to the Government House Leaders of the two Opposition Parties sent to them on January 28, 1985, outlining what the Government is proposing and seeking the views of the two Opposition House Leaders. As yet the Government has not heard from the two Opposition House Leaders and has not been able to go ahead.
The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) indicated that he was worried at the initial stage that this matter would be forged ahead unilaterally. Obviously his initial concerns were wrong and his present concern is wrong. It has not been forged ahead unilaterally. It has never been threatened that it would go ahead unilaterally.

There has not been any agreement, Mr. Speaker. That is the reason the matter has not gone ahead. Before the Hon. Member was suggesting that there should not be artifi-

May 21, 1985
Adjournment Debate
cial deadlines to bring it to conclusion, but he is now asking in his statement this evening to bring the matter to a conclusion. That in itself is a contradiction. I would suggest these matters continue in discussion. Hopefully all Parties will find a consensus to allow this matter to be resolved. On Wednesday, May 15, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism met with Mr. Miki. They had amicable discussions at that time. At that time they agreed that an apology was necessary. Discussion at the present time centre around what appropriate redress, if any, there should be.
Compensation was not originally considered as the appropriate word and we have now heard various descriptions of what compensation may be, which defies any definition which is precise. We do not want this matter to go into an auction. The
Government wants the matter to be dealt with as a moral issue and to give some emphasis to the people who have suffered and to the Japanese Canadian community that matters of this type will not happen again in Canada.
Other than that, I would suggest that the Hon. Member should read the letter dated January 28, 1985 and perhaps encourage his House Leader and the House Leader of the Official Opposition to respond to the letter of the Government House Leader.
